# Heaven and Earth

<margin>
Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). This refers to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian philosopher, whose commentaries became the standard for the imperial examinations.</note> says:
</margin>

> Only Heaven is truly great; only the Ruler is most venerable.
> Governance and moral education originate in human principles,
> while auspicious signs and strange transformations are revealed in the patterns of the stars <note>original: "天文" (tianwen). In this context, it refers to both physical astronomy and the astrological signs interpreted as messages from the divine.</note>.
> If one’s conduct has flaws or imperfections <note>original: "玷玦" (dianjue). Literally a "stain" or "crack" in a piece of ceremonial jade, used here as a metaphor for moral failings.</note>, then the celestial images will show it.
> If Heaven produces ominous portents <note>original: "妖孽" (yaonie). Refers to unnatural phenomena or disasters seen as warnings to a ruler.</note>, then one’s virtue should be renewed daily.
> That which is firmly established above and brilliantly clear is the **substance of Heaven**.
> That which is substantial below and peaceful and still is the **form of the Earth**.

### Technical Vocabulary

**Master Zhu** <note>The posthumous title of Zhu Xi, the central figure of the School of Principle.</note>
**Governance and Education** <note>The dual role of the state: to provide order and to cultivate the morality of the people.</note>
**Celestial Phenomena** <note>The observation of the heavens to understand the "Will of Heaven."</note>
**Flaws and Imperfections** <note>Moral defects in a leader that disrupt the natural harmony.</note>
**Ominous Portents** <note>Natural disasters or strange sightings interpreted as divine rebukes.</note>
**Daily Renewal** <note>A core Confucian concept of constant self-cultivation and improvement.</note>
**Substance of Heaven** <note>The essential, spiritual, and physical nature of the cosmos.</note>
**Form of the Earth** <note>The physical, stable, and receptive nature of the terrestrial world.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the fundamental Confucian concept of the "Unity of Heaven and Humanity," quoting Master Zhu Xi to explain how the behavior of rulers is reflected in celestial events. It establishes a moral cosmology where the stars serve as a mirror for the ethics of the earthly government.</summary>

<keywords>Zhu Xi, Neo-Confucianism, Heaven and Earth, Mandate of Heaven, omens, morality, cosmology, governance</keywords>

# Divination on Sudden Changes in the Sky

**A landscape illustration depicting rugged mountain peaks and trees under an ominous, dark grey sky. The heavy clouds suggest a sudden atmospheric change, reflecting the subject of the divination title above.**

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to the great Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi.</note> says: If the color of the sky suddenly changes, the surrounding tribes <note>original: "四夷" (Siyi). Historically translated as the "Four Barbarians," referring to non-Han peoples surrounding the Chinese heartland.</note> will come to invade.

The *Annals of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Likely referring to the astronomical or "Five Elements" treatises within the official History of the Song Dynasty.</note> says: A sudden change in the sky’s color is called the "Black Constant" <note>original: "黑常" (Heichang). A technical term for an unnatural, persistent darkening of the sky viewed as a dire omen.</note>. It signifies that the surrounding tribes will come to invade.

The *Great Plan* <note>original: "洪範" (Hong Fan). A classic text from the *Book of Documents* which correlates human behavior with natural phenomena.</note> says: Clarity and brightness are the essential substance of Heaven. A sudden change in the sky’s color is called the "Black Constant."

<column-break/>

# Divination on Sudden Sinking of the Earth

**A landscape painting showing green-peaked mountains and a valley with two small buildings. The ground in the foreground near the houses is depicted with dark lines indicating cracks or subsidence, visually representing the "sinking earth" omen.**

Master Zhu says: If the earth suddenly sinks, the myriad people will be scattered and dispersed.

The *Annals of Song* says: When the earth sinks, it means subordinate officials are monopolizing power. The myriad people will be scattered; it also signifies the loss of territory.

Jing Fang <note>A Han dynasty scholar (77–37 BCE) famous for his system of interpreting the *I Ching* to predict disasters.</note> says: If a mountain sinks of its own accord without cause, military conflict will arise throughout the world.

Fan Ye’s <note>The historian (398–445 CE) who compiled the *Book of the Later Han*.</note> *Book of Han* says: The sinking of the earth signifies that the royal house is in chaos and high ministers are monopolizing governance.

### Technical Vocabulary

**Sinking Earth** <note>original: "地陷" (Dixian). Geological subsidence interpreted as a sign of collapsing social or political stability.</note>
**Sky Color** <note>original: "天色" (Tianse). The appearance of the heavens, which was monitored for signs of the "Will of Heaven."</note>
**Master Zhu** <note>Zhu Xi, whose philosophy integrated natural observation with moral governance.</note>
**Annals of Song** <note>An official dynastic history used as a reference for historical omens.</note>
**Jing Fang** <note>An expert in Yi Jing (Book of Changes) divination and astronomical omens.</note>
**Fan Ye** <note>The primary author of the *Book of the Later Han*.</note>
**Book of Han** <note>An official history covering the Han Dynasty, often cited for its records of strange portents.</note>
**The Great Plan** <note>A foundational text of Chinese political philosophy and cosmology.</note>
**Monopolizing Power** <note>original: "專政" (Zhuanzheng). An official or minister ruling without the Emperor’s consent.</note>
**Scattered and Dispersed** <note>original: "離散" (Lisan). The displacement of the population, usually due to war or famine.</note>
**Military Conflict** <note>original: "兵作" (Bingzuo). Literally "the rising of weapons" or the start of a war.</note>
**Surrounding Tribes** <note>The "Four Barbarians" of the cardinal directions.</note>
**Black Constant** <note>A specific atmospheric phenomenon signaling impending doom.</note>

<summary>This page lists divinations regarding sudden atmospheric and geological changes, interpreting them as omens of foreign invasion and domestic political corruption. It draws on authorities like Zhu Xi and the Book of Han to warn that natural disasters reflect a breakdown in the ruler's authority.</summary>
<keywords>divination, omens, Zhu Xi, Jing Fang, political corruption, foreign invasion, Black Constant, sinking earth</keywords>

# General Omens of Earthquakes

**A traditional Chinese landscape illustration framed within a black border. At the top of the border, the title "General Omens of Earthquakes" is inscribed. The painting depicts rocky mountains in ink and light blue/brown washes, with sparse trees and two traditional buildings with dark tiled roofs. Below the image is a block of vertical Chinese text.**

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to the influential Neo-Confucian scholar Zhu Xi (1130–1200).</note> says: An earthquake means there is an excess of <term>Yin (the receptive or "shadow" principle associated with ministers and the earth)</term>. It signifies that ministers are usurping the ruler's power and that war will break out.

The *Annals of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Likely referring to the astronomical or "Five Elements" treatises within the official History of the Song Dynasty.</note> says: When the earth shakes, it is said that the ministers are too strong. <term>Yang (the active or "light" principle associated with the ruler and the sun)</term> is hidden and cannot emerge; *Yin* is compressed and cannot enter. This indicates an excess of *Yin*. If the maternal relatives of the emperor seize power or if the empresses and consorts interfere in government, the earth will undergo these strange changes. Likewise, if those below plot against those above or if the common people are disturbed, the earth will shake.

In terms of the broader divination, it signifies great military chaos. Regarding the seasons: in spring, the year will not be prosperous; in summer, the ruler will be filled with anxiety and the five grains <note>The five staple crops of ancient China, representing the food supply.</note> will be damaged; in autumn, war will arise; in winter, the towns will be burdened by major construction projects <note>original: "土功" (tugong). This usually refers to forced labor for walls or fortifications.</note>.

The *Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* <note>original: "春秋傳" (Chunqiu Zhuan).</note> says: Bo Yangfu <note>A famous court official and diviner of the Western Zhou Dynasty.</note> stated: When the <term>Qi (the vital energy or life force)</term> of Heaven and Earth loses its proper order, it leads to long-term chaos. *Yang* is hidden and cannot emerge; *Yin* is compressed and cannot enter; thus, there is an earthquake.

<column-break/>

# Omens of Heaven Splitting

**A traditional Chinese landscape illustration framed within a black border. At the top of the border, the title "Omens of Heaven Splitting" is inscribed. The painting shows green and brown mountain peaks under a pale sky. A large, curved, white arc representing a rift in the sky spans across the landscape. Below the image is a block of vertical Chinese text, sparsely arranged.**

Master Zhu says: A "splitting of the sky" signifies a deficiency of *Yang*. It means the ruler is weak and the ministers are causing chaos; thus, the sky splits.

The *Annals of Song* say: A rift in the sky signifies a deficiency of *Yang*. It means the ministers are in rebellion and the ruler has lost the <term>Way (the Dao, or the moral path of righteous governance)</term>. As a result, the land itself will soon split.

Ban Gu’s *History of the Han* <note>original: "班固漢書" (Ban Gu Hanshu). An essential historical record of the Western Han Dynasty written in the 1st century AD.</note> says: A rift in the sky and a deficiency of *Yang* are both signs of subordinates becoming too powerful and prosperous, which is an omen that they will eventually harm the ruler.

<summary>This page explains that earthquakes and rifts in the sky are not merely natural disasters, but warnings of political imbalance, specifically when ministers or imperial consorts become too powerful at the expense of a weak ruler. It draws on classical historical and philosophical sources to link geological and celestial stability to the moral and administrative "Way" of the government.</summary>

<keywords>earthquake, celestial rift, Yin and Yang, Zhu Xi, political omens, Han Dynasty history, Song Dynasty history, ministerial rebellion, corruption, Bo Yangfu, Qi, the Dao</keywords>

### Divination of Earthquakes and Floods | Divination of Land Subsidence

**[Image: A landscape illustration depicting the divination for earthquakes and floods. Raging white waves fill the lower portion of the frame, with the dark roof of a single house visible floating upon them. In the background, craggy mountain peaks rise through a thick layer of mist and clouds.]**

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晉書" (Jin Shu). An official historical record of the Jin Dynasty, compiled in the 7th century, which includes detailed records of natural portents and their political meanings.</note> says:

Earthquakes and floods arise when the path of <term>Yin (the dark, receptive, or subordinate principle)</term> flourishes as a response to the obstruction of <term>Yang (the bright, active, or sovereign principle)</term>.

<column-break/>

**[Image: A landscape illustration depicting the divination for land subsidence. At the base of a large, shadowed mountain, traditional buildings are shown sinking into the ground. To the right of the houses stands a tall, monolithic stone tower or pillar on a patch of level ground near a body of water.]**

Fan Ye <note>original: "范曄" (398–445 AD). A scholar and historian of the Liu Song dynasty, primarily known for compiling the *Book of the Later Han*.</note> says:

The sinking of the earth signifies that the royal court is in a state of chaos. The sinking of a tower <note>original: "塔" (Ta). This refers to a pagoda or ceremonial tower, which represented the stability and spiritual height of the civilization.</note> signifies that high-ranking ministers are usurping political power.

<summary>This page correlates geological disasters like earthquakes and land subsidence with specific political failures, such as the collapse of royal authority and the overstepping of government ministers.</summary>
<keywords>Earthquakes, Floods, Land Subsidence, Book of Jin, Fan Ye, Yin and Yang, Political Corruption, Omens</keywords>

### Divination of Earthquakes Affecting Houses

**[Image: A traditional Chinese landscape painting in ink and light color. In the foreground, several small houses with tiled roofs are nestled among trees. In the background, there are rolling hills and a prominent mountain peak rendered with blue and green washes. The water or mist in the distance is suggested by empty space and light brushstrokes.]**

Ban Gu <note>original: "班固" (32–92 AD). A renowned historian and poet of the Han Dynasty, primarily responsible for compiling the *Book of Han*.</note> in the *Book of Han* <note>original: "漢書" (Han Shu). One of the "Four Histories" of the Chinese canon, covering the Western Han period.</note> says:

When an earthquake causes the tiles of a house to fall, it signifies that subordinates are becoming excessively powerful and are about to move to cause harm.

<column-break/>

### Divination of Earthly Rumblings

**[Image: A landscape illustration depicting a man in traditional robes standing in an open area, looking toward distant mountains. The scene is atmospheric, with dark, heavy clouds swirling in the sky above the hills. To the left and right are sparse, gnarled trees. The overall mood suggests a significant natural or celestial phenomenon.]**

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent scholar of Neo-Confucianism whose commentaries became the basis of the imperial examinations.</note> says:

When the earth rumbles with a sound like rustling grain <note>original: "有穀" (you gu). This describes a specific acoustic phenomenon where the earth produces a sound reminiscent of grain being moved or shaken, viewed as a warning of instability.</note>, the <term>Son of Heaven (the Emperor)</term> has lost control of the governance of the state.

The *History of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Specifically referring to the "Treatises" within the official history of the Song Dynasty, which record portents and their meanings.</note> says:

When the earth rumbles with a sound like rustling grain, the <term>Son of Heaven</term> has lost control of the governance of the state because he has granted too much power to women <note>original: "任婦女" (ren funü). In the context of traditional Chinese political theory, the "usurpation" of power by women at court was seen as a manifestation of unbalanced *Yin* energy, often predicted by geological disturbances.</note>.

<summary>This page details how specific earthquake effects, like falling roof tiles or mysterious subterranean sounds, serve as omens for political instability, particularly the rise of ambitious subordinates or the undue influence of women in the imperial court.</summary>
<keywords>Ban Gu, Book of Han, Zhu Xi, History of Song, earthquakes, terrestrial rumblings, political portents, Son of Heaven, Yin and Yang</keywords>

# Divination of Earthquakes at the Ancestral Temple

**[Image: A woodblock print illustration in ink and light color depicting a courtyard of an ancestral temple during an earthquake. In the center, an official in a formal red robe and black winged cap kneels on the ground, likely in prayer or submission to the divine omen. To the right, a section of a white-walled building with a tiled roof is severely damaged and leaning precariously. A tall, sparsely-leaved tree stands to the left. Mountains and foliage are visible in the background under a light wash of color. The entire scene is enclosed within a rectangular border.]**

<margin>The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Refers to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *Book of Song*, a historical record of the Liu Song dynasty (420–479 AD).</note> says:</margin>
When an earthquake occurs at the ancestral temples <term>Ancestral Temple: 宗廟 (Zongmiao). A sacred hall where the spirits of deceased rulers or family ancestors are honored; damage here was seen as a direct threat to the dynasty's legitimacy.</term> or palace chambers and the shaking does not cease, the state harbors rebellious officials. Slanderous sycophants <term>Sycophants: 讒佞 (Channing). Smooth-talking flatterers who deceive the ruler to gain power.</term> are being promoted, and high ministers are plotting revolt; if they move to act, they shall be executed. Punishment is meted out to those below according to reason, yet those above and below are not in harmony. The need for reform or the cause of the trouble lies with the women <note>This likely refers to the "inner court," specifically the influence of empresses or concubines over state affairs, seen as an inversion of the natural order.</note>.

The *Commentary on the Book of Changes by Jing Fang* <note>original: "京房易傳" (Jing Fang Yi Zhuan). Jing Fang (77–37 BC) was a famous Han dynasty scholar who developed systems of divination to interpret natural disasters as political warnings.</note> says:
When an earthquake strikes the ancestral temple, there are rebellious subordinates in the cities and chaotic officials in the state; the shaking will not stop.

<column-break/>

# Divination of Earthquakes as Ominous Calamities

**[Image: A woodblock print illustration of a desolate natural landscape, representing a disaster omen. A large, rounded hill or mound is the central feature on the right side. Several leafless trees are scattered across an uneven terrain rendered with sharp, jagged ink strokes, suggesting ground tremors or the earth cracking open. In the foreground, small patches of grass grow on the broken earth. There are no human figures or structures in this scene, emphasizing the raw, disruptive power of nature.]**

<margin>Fan Ye <note>original: "范曄" (398–445 AD). The primary compiler of the *Book of the Later Han*, known for documenting portents and omens.</note> says:</margin>
The Earth is *Yin* <note>original: "陰" (Yin). In Chinese philosophy, the feminine, passive, and receptive principle.</note>; it is meant to remain tranquil. If it oversteps its *Yin* duties and usurps the governing role of *Yang* <note>original: "陽" (Yang). The masculine, active principle associated with the Sun and the Ruler.</note>, the world responds with a tremor.

The *Commentary by Jing Fang* says:
The Earth represents the station of the high ministers. It should safely support the myriad people and nourish all things. When it trembles and shakes, it signifies that the ministers are failing to provide safety and support for the people and the ten thousand things on behalf of the sovereign.

<summary>This page interprets earthquakes occurring at sacred ancestral temples and palaces as omens of political rebellion and court corruption. It uses the Yin-Yang framework to explain that a shaking Earth represents ministers or women overstepping their rightful, passive roles to usurp the active authority of the ruler.</summary>
<keywords>Earthquakes, Ancestral Temples, Jing Fang, Omen Divination, Yin and Yang, Rebellious Officials, Han Dynasty Philosophy, Palace Intrigue</keywords>

# Divination of Sky Rifts where People Appear
# Divination of Earthquakes and the Behavior of Birds and Livestock

[Image: A watercolor illustration of a jagged mountain landscape with small bamboo plants. In the upper left corner, in a pale sky, four human figures in long dark robes are depicted walking in a line. A rocky cliff face rises on the right side.]

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晉書" (Jin Shu). An official historical record compiled in 648 AD covering the history of the Jin dynasty (266–420 AD).</note> says:

A rift in the sky where human figures appear is an omen of war rising <term>War rising: 兵起 (Bingqi). Literally "soldiers arising," referring to the outbreak of rebellion or military conflict.</term> and the downfall of the nation.

<column-break/>

[Image: A watercolor illustration showing a white horse and a dark brown ox running frantically across a landscape with trees and hills. Small grey brushstrokes near the trees and animals represent falling debris and the movement of the earth, signifying an earthquake.]

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Refers to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *Book of Song*, which records natural anomalies as signs of political heaven-sent warnings.</note> says:

If cattle, horses, birds, and beasts flee in panic, there will be hardship regarding the grain harvests <term>Hardship regarding grain: 黍患 (Shuhuan). Specifically referring to millet, the staple crop; this indicates impending famine or agricultural failure.</term>.

Jing Fang’s *Transformations of the Changes* <note>original: "京房易妖" (Jing Fang Yi Yao). A specialized text by the Han dynasty scholar Jing Fang, who used the *I Ching* (Book of Changes) to interpret natural disasters as "monsters" or "anomalies" caused by political failings.</note> says:

When an earthquake occurs and cattle, horses, birds, and beasts [are driven to flight], the Son of Heaven <term>Son of Heaven: 天子 (Tianzi). The Emperor, whose legitimacy was believed to be maintained by his harmony with the natural world.</term> shall lose his position.

<summary>This page describes two dire omens: the appearance of figures in a "split sky," signifying national collapse, and the panicked flight of animals during earthquakes, which foretells famine and the Emperor's loss of power.</summary>
<keywords>celestial omens, sky rift, earthquakes, animal behavior, Book of Jin, Jing Fang, political legitimacy, famine</keywords>

# Divination of Grass Raining from the Sky

[Image: A traditional Chinese landscape painting in shades of green, blue, and grey. Dark, feathery strokes representing falling grass descend diagonally from the upper left sky toward a cluster of jagged mountains.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential philosopher of the Neo-Confucian tradition.</note> says:
The anomaly of grass raining from the sky is caused by the decline of official rewards and public trust <term>Official rewards and trust: 禄信 (Luxin). In traditional Chinese cosmology, the moral integrity of the government—specifically how it distributes salaries (lu) and maintains its word (xin)—is believed to affect the balance of nature.</term>.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). This refers to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *Book of Song*, a historical record that interprets natural disasters as heavenly warnings to the Emperor.</note> says:
The anomaly of grass raining from the sky is caused by the decline of official rewards and public trust. This is known as "Heaven losing its nature." When the sky rains red grass, the people will be displaced and forced to wander <term>Displaced: 流 (liu). Referring to the movement of refugees fleeing their homes due to war, famine, or social collapse.</term>.

Xun Yue’s *Annals of Han* <note>original: "荀悅漢書" (Xun Yue Hanshu). Referring to the *Han Ji*, a history by the scholar Xun Yue (148–209 AD) which summarized the earlier *Book of Han*.</note> says:
When the sky rains grass, it signifies that ministers are monopolizing government power <term>Monopolizing power: 專政 (zhuanzheng). A situation where subordinates or officials have usurped the rightful authority of the ruler.</term>. The grass resembles nut grass <note>original: "菠莎" (bosuo). Likely *Cyperus rotundus*, a common weed often used in traditional medicine.</note>, tangled and knotted together like round pellets.

<column-break/>

# Divination of the Sky Roaring with Sound

[Image: A traditional Chinese landscape painting depicting a stormy, dark grey sky swirling above a hilly terrain. A man dressed in a blue robe stands on a path, looking up at the heavens with one hand raised, as if reacting to a great sound.]

Master Zhu says:
When the sky roars with sound, the ruler of men will experience sorrow and alarm.

The *Treatise of Song* says:
When the sky roars with sound, the ruler of men will experience sorrow and alarm. The common people will be exhausted by labor and lose their ancestral lands.

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晋書" (Jin Shu). The official historical record of the Jin Dynasty (266–420 AD), compiled in the 7th century.</note> says:
When the sky roars with sound, the *Yin* energy is flourishing while the *Yang* energy is weak <term>Yin and Yang: 陰陽 (Yin Yang). The two fundamental forces of the universe. In political terms, an excess of Yin (dark, passive, cold) over Yang (light, active, warm) often symbolized a weak emperor and the rise of treacherous "dark" influences in the court.</term>. The ruler of men will grieve.

<summary>This page describes the omens of "grass rain" and "sky roaring," interpreting them as divine reactions to government corruption, the loss of imperial authority, and the suffering of the common people.</summary>
<keywords>celestial omens, grass rain, sky roar, Zhu Xi, Book of Song, Book of Han, Book of Jin, Yin and Yang, political corruption, displacement</keywords>

# Divination of Earth Growing Hair

[Image: A colored woodblock-style illustration of a rocky mountain landscape. Fine vertical black lines are depicted emerging from the ground among the grass and rocks, representing the phenomenon of "earth growing hair."]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name for Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the renowned Neo-Confucian scholar whose commentaries became the basis for imperial examinations.</note> says:
The earth growing hair is a sign of the people's exhaustion and the onset of military conflict.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Specifically the "Treatise on the Five Elements" from the *Book of Song*, which records anomalies as political warnings.</note> says:
The earth growing hair occurs when Metal loses its nature <term>Metal: 金 (jin). One of the Five Elements in Chinese cosmology. It represents justice, harvest, and the West; when it "loses its nature," the moral and physical order of the state is said to collapse.</term>; the people will soon face great toil.

The *Earth Mirror* <note>original: "地鏡" (Di Jing). An ancient, largely lost text on divination and the interpretation of terrestrial omens.</note> says:
If the earth grows hair, the world will fall into chaos and armies will rise.

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晉書" (Jin Shu). The official history of the Jin Dynasty (266–420 AD).</note> says:
When Metal loses its nature, the earth grows hair. The people will be burdened with labor, and the military will find no peace.

<column-break/>

# Divination of Stones Raining from the Sky

[Image: A colored woodblock-style illustration showing black stones falling from dark, swirling clouds in the sky. A person in a pink robe is shown in the foreground running toward a mountain for safety. The scene is set in a landscape with jagged rocks and trees.]

Master Zhu says:
Stones raining from the heavens signify a great battle and misfortune for the ruler.

The *Treatise of Song* says:
The sky raining stones indicates that trust is not being practiced, while deceit and falsehood are flourishing among the subordinates; the ruler will face calamity. Stones that fall within a foot of the ground and resemble chicken eggs—especially those with sharp tips—are called "Heavenly Drums" <note>original: "天鼓" (tiangu). These are interpreted as the physical manifestation of heavenly wrath or the sound of divine drums signaling war.</note>. They appeared during the final suppression of the Yin <note>original: "殷討" (Yintao). Referring to the conquest of the Shang/Yin Dynasty by King Wu of Zhou.</note>. It is also recorded that stones as large as water vats rained down when King Wu led his campaign of punishment.

Fan Ye’s *Book of Han* <note>original: "范曄漢書" (Fan Ye Hanshu). Usually referring to the *Book of the Later Han* (Hou Han Shu), compiled by the historian Fan Ye (398–445 AD).</note> says:
Stones raining from the high heavens down to the earth is an omen of the people’s distress and hardship.

<summary>This page lists omens involving "earth hair" and "falling stones," interpreting them as signs of social exhaustion, government deception, and imminent regime change. It references historical precedents like the fall of the Shang Dynasty to validate these supernatural warnings.</summary>
<keywords>Earth Growing Hair, Raining Stones, Five Elements, Metal Element, Zhu Xi, Book of Song, King Wu of Zhou, Heavenly Drums, military omens, political corruption</keywords>

# Divination of Overcast and Gloomy Skies

[Image: An ink wash landscape illustration within a rectangular border. Dark, dense clouds hang low over a range of mountains. Trees and rocky outcrops in the foreground are painted with dark, heavy ink, creating a somber, overcast atmosphere typical of traditional Chinese literati painting.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), whose Neo-Confucian philosophy integrated natural phenomena with moral governance.</note> says:

When the sky is overcast and gloomy but it does not rain, it signifies internal rebellion and the hatching of secret plots and conspiracies.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). The "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *Book of Song*, which records celestial and terrestrial portents.</note> says:

When the sky suddenly becomes dark and gloomy by day and night—so that the sun is not seen by day and the stars and moon are not seen by night—it indicates a secret plot. One interpretation says this represents internal rebellion, where those below plot against those above. If it rains, it suggests that the enemies are of equal strength and are secretly conspiring against one another.

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晉書" (Jin Shu). The official history of the Jin Dynasty, covering the years 266–420 AD.</note> says:

If the sky remains dark and gloomy through both day and night, then those in subordinate positions are engaged in secret plotting.

<column-break/>

# Divination of Springs Forming in the Earth

[Image: An ink wash landscape illustration within a rectangular border. A powerful torrent of water erupts from the side of a rocky hill, gushing across the center of the frame. The scene includes stylized trees and distant mountain peaks under a pale sky.]

Master Zhu says:

When the earth produces springs, it foretells great floods and military chaos.

The *Treatise of Song* says:

When the earth forms springs of its own accord without cause, the world will fall into chaos and armies will rise. There will be great floods.

<term>Overcast and Gloomy: 陰晦 (yinhui). In traditional cosmology, "Yin" represents the dark, cold, and subordinate principle. Excessive "Yin" in the sky (darkness) suggests that the "Yin" elements of society (ministers or commoners) are overstepping their bounds to eclipse the "Yang" (the Emperor/Sun).</term>

<term>Secret Plotting: 陰謀 (yinmou). Literally "Yin schemes." This refers to clandestine activities or treachery hidden from the light of the sovereign's authority.</term>

<summary>This page interprets persistent atmospheric darkness and spontaneous springs as ominous signs of internal conspiracies, impending rebellions, and devastating floods. These natural anomalies are presented as direct warnings of a breakdown in the hierarchical order between the ruler and the ruled.</summary>

<keywords>Zhu Xi, Book of Song, Book of Jin, omens, rebellion, secret plots, floods, Yin and Yang, atmospheric divination, groundwater anomalies</keywords>

# Divination of Mountain Roaring

[Image: A traditional Chinese landscape painting in ink and color. It depicts mountains and valleys with a single figure in a green robe standing in the foreground, looking up towards the peaks as if listening to the mountains. The sky is a pale wash, and the terrain is rendered with soft brushwork.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referencing Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian philosopher, who believed natural disasters were "remonstrances" from Heaven to the Emperor.</note> says:

When a mountain roars, there will be great chaos.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Specifically the "Treatise on the Five Elements" from the *Book of Song*.</note> says:

When a mountain roars, there will be great chaos.

The *Mirror of the Earth* <note>original: "地鏡" (Di Jing). An ancient, now largely lost, manual on terrestrial divination and prospecting.</note> says:

If a mountain makes a cracking sound <note>original: "殼" (ke). While literally "shell," in this context it refers to the sharp sound of cracking or hulling.</note> by day or night, there will be war and mourning throughout the world.

Fan Ye’s *Book of Han* <note>original: "范曄漢書" (Fan Ye Han Shu). Also known as the *Book of the Later Han*.</note> says:

When a great mountain roars frequently, with a sound as loud as the lowing of an ox, it is an omen that the world will be split into four parts and torn into five pieces <note>A metaphor for total national disintegration and civil war.</note>.

# Divination of the Earth Splitting

[Image: A traditional Chinese landscape painting showing a desolate, cracked landscape. Broad fissures run through the earth, and sparse, leafless trees are scattered across the rocky ground. In the background, low hills rise under a grey, overcast sky, conveying a sense of geological upheaval.]

Master Zhu says:

When the earth splits open and produces a sound, high-ranking ministers will lose their positions and the world will not be at peace.

The *Treatise of Song* says:

When the weather of winter is felt in the autumn, the earth will split. This corresponds to the separation of the scholars and the commoners. High-ranking ministers will become tyrannical and self-indulgent; those below will rebel against those above. The worthy will retire from public life, while the unworthy will advance. If the earth splits and makes a sound, there will be no peace in any of the four directions, great armies will arise, and the state will lose its territory.

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晉書" (Jin Shu). The official history of the Jin Dynasty (266–420 AD).</note> says:

The splitting of the earth signifies that subordinates are drifting away and no longer following their superiors. Li Gu <note>A famous scholar-official of the Eastern Han known for his integrity and his interpretations of omens.</note> believed this to be an omen of the "Yin-kind" <term>Yin-kind (陰類): Referring to those in subordinate or traditionally "passive" positions—such as ministers, subjects, or even the imperial harem—usurping power.</term> becoming tyrannical and arrogant, a sign of impending separation.

<summary>This page records divinations regarding geological anomalies, interpreting the "roaring" of mountains and the "splitting" of the earth as dire omens of civil war, the advancement of corrupt officials, and the ultimate disintegration of the state.</summary>
<keywords>Mountain Roaring, Earth Splitting, Zhu Xi, Book of Song, Book of Jin, Li Gu, Omens, Political Instability, Disintegration</keywords>

# Divination of Earth Burning

[Image: A landscape illustration depicting mountains and trees under a pale sky. Jagged red flames rise from various points on the ground and hillsides, suggesting the earth itself is burning.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent philosopher of the Neo-Confucian tradition.</note> says:

Earth burning is a disaster born of unchecked arrogance and self-inflicted harm.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Specifically the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *Book of Song*, a historical record of the 5th-century Liu Song dynasty.</note> says:

Regarding the phenomenon of earth burning: Fire is the essence of *Yang* <term>Yang: the active, bright, and masculine principle associated here with the Ruler</term>, while Earth is the master of *Yin* <term>Yin: the receptive, dark, and feminine principle associated here with the Ministers</term>. If the earth burns, it signifies a violation of the Way of *Yin* and the improper exercise of *Yang* governance. This is an omen of injury without conquest; it signifies ministers who act with arbitrary power and ultimately bring about their own destruction.

The *Astronomical Records* <note>original: "天文錄" (Tianwen Lu). An ancient compendium documenting celestial and terrestrial omens.</note> says:

Fire is the essence of *Yang*, and Earth is the master of *Yin*, for it is the earth that supports all living things. When the earth burns, it represents a transgression of the Way of *Yin* and the execution of *Yang* authority. This is an omen of injury without conquest. It does not merely signify the scorching of living creatures, but portends self-inflicted death. *Yang* represents the path of the Sovereign, and *Yin* represents the path of the Minister. When subordinates seize power and act with total license, they will ultimately cause their own downfall.

<column-break/>

# Divination of the Heavenly Drum

[Image: A celestial phenomenon is depicted in a dark, cloudy sky. A large, thick circular ring with four dark rectangular fittings (representing a "heavenly drum") floats above a landscape of hills and coniferous trees.]

Master Zhu says:

The Heavenly Drum signifies the presence of violent troops.

The *Treatise of Song* says:

Thunder that sounds when there are no clouds is named the "Heavenly Drum." It signifies that violent troops will <gloss>arise</gloss>.

Jing Fang <note>original: "京房" (77–37 BCE). A scholar of the Han dynasty famous for his expertise in the *I Ching* and his theories on the relationship between musical pitch and climate.</note> says:

When there is thunder in the sky during the day without clouds, this is called the "Heavenly Drum." The nation over which this occurs will surely face armed soldiers, and the state’s leadership will be left hollow and weak.

<summary>This page describes two terrestrial and atmospheric portents: fires emerging from the ground (Earth Burning) and thunder in clear skies (Heavenly Drum), both interpreted as signs of ministerial overreach and imminent military conflict.</summary>

# Divination of Heavenly Fire

[Image: An illustration depicting "Heavenly Fire." Swirls of orange and red flames descend through dark grey smoke clouds onto the tiled roof of a traditional Chinese structure.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent philosopher of the Neo-Confucian tradition.</note> says:

Heavenly fire is a warning against hypocrisy and debauchery.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Specifically the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *Book of Song*, which records natural anomalies and their political meanings.</note> says:

The disaster of heavenly fire occurs when fire does not flare upward <note>In the system of the Five Elements, the natural property of fire is to rise (炎上). Fire falling from the sky represents a violation of the natural order.</note>. It manifests when faith in the Way is not sincere, and when there is a hollow pursuit of vanity and the building of palaces without restraint. Then, this disaster appears and burns the ancestral temples <term>Ancestral temples: "Zongmiao" (宗廟), the most sacred buildings in the realm where the spirits of the ruling family's ancestors were housed; their destruction symbolized the end of a dynasty's legitimacy.</term>.

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晋書" (Jin Shu). The official historical record of the Jin Dynasty (266–420 AD).</note> says: When the ruler raises his terraces too high, Heaven sends fire as a disaster.

# Divination of Earth Gushing Soil like Mountains | Divination of Sky Raining Soil and Haze

[Image: A woodblock illustration on the left page showing a large dark mound of earth or stone rising abruptly from the ground, illustrating the omen "Earth Gushing Soil like Mountains." The image is framed within a rectangular border, with descriptive text below it.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the influential Neo-Confucian scholar.</note> says:

When subordinates are about to rise up in rebellion, the earth gushes soil like mountains.

The *Book of Tang* <note>original: "唐書" (Tang Shu). The official historical record of the Tang Dynasty.</note> says:

The official Yu Wenjun <note>Yu Wenjun was a Tang official who famously interpreted the sudden appearance of a hill as a sign of divine displeasure during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian.</note> submitted a memorial saying: 

"When the weather is out of harmony, the heat and cold are separated. When the human *qi* <term>Qi: (氣) the vital energy or life-force that flows through all things; here it refers to the health of the social body.</term> is out of harmony, tumors and boils grow. When the earth's *qi* is out of harmony, mounds and hillocks emerge. Now, the Empress <note>Refers to Wu Zetian (r. 690–705), the only woman to rule China as an emperor in her own right. Her reign was often criticized by traditional historians using these omens.</note> occupies the male position; this reversal of the *Yang* <note>original: "陽" (Yang). The masculine, active principle associated with the Sun and the Emperor.</note> results in weakness. Thus, the earth's energy is blocked and obstructed, causing mountains to transform into disasters."

<column-break/>

[Image: A woodblock illustration on the right page depicting several mountain peaks shrouded in a reddish-brown haze or falling dust, illustrating the omen "Sky Raining Soil and Haze." The sky is filled with a light wash of color to suggest the atmospheric phenomenon. Descriptive text is provided below the image within a frame.]

Master Zhu says:

When the common people are exhausted by labor and the unworthy receive salaries, the sky rains with soil and haze <term>Haze: "Mai" (霾). In ancient contexts, this refers to dust storms or wind-borne soil that darkens the sky, rather than modern industrial smog.</term>.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Likely the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *Book of Song*.</note> says:

When the sky rains soil, it is called haze. It indicates that the ruler has lost their proper nature and the people are overworked, or that those without merit are receiving official salaries.

*Mozi* <note>original: "墨子". An ancient text of the Mohist school, which emphasized meritocracy and criticized wasteful governance.</note> says:

Because King Zhou of Shang <note>The last ruler of the Shang Dynasty, traditionally depicted as a quintessential tyrant.</note> lacked virtue, in the tenth month, soil rained as haze upon the capital of Bo.

The *Book of Tang* says:

When the unworthy are granted salaries, the sky rains soil. It also says: this occurs when the common people are exhausted by labor.

<summary>This page describes two terrestrial and atmospheric omens—spontaneous earth mounds and falling dust—linking them to the "unnatural" political power of Empress Wu Zetian and the economic exhaustion of the peasantry.</summary>
<keywords>Earth Gushing Soil, Sky Raining Soil, Haze, Empress Wu Zetian, Yu Wenjun, Book of Tang, Master Zhu, political omens, social disharmony</keywords>

# Divination of the Sky Raining Ice on Trees | Divination of Strange Lights Arising from the Earth

[Image: A woodcut-style illustration with light ink and watercolor washes depicting a storm. Dark grey clouds fill the upper part of the frame. Heavy diagonal streaks of rain lash against three sparse trees, which bend to the left under the force of the wind. The branches of the trees appear thick and coated in a layer of white ice or frozen glaze.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian philosopher.</note> says:

When a person of high rank is about to die, it rains ice upon the trees until they appear as if clad in armor.

The *Treatise of the Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Likely referring to the "Treatise on Five Elements" within the *History of the Song Dynasty*.</note> says:

When it rains on the trees and that rain turns to ice, it is because high ministers harbor *Yin* <term>Yin: (陰) the principle of darkness, cold, and passivity; in a political context, it often represents the influence of subordinates or the empress over the emperor.</term> energy. This energy clings to the wood; therefore, the trees freeze.

The *Commentary on the Great Plan* <note>original: "洪範傳" (Hong Fan Zhuan). An ancient commentary on a chapter of the *Book of Documents* that correlates human behavior with natural phenomena.</note> says:

Ice is also known by the name "Armor" <note>original: "介" (jie). This term can mean scales, shells, or military armor.</note>, which is a symbolic omen of warfare.

Ban Gu’s <note>Ban Gu (32–92 AD) was the primary author of the *Book of Han*.</note> *Book of Han* says:

When the sky rains ice on the trees, an empress or consort will pass away, or ministers will initiate a rebellion.

<column-break/>

[Image: A woodcut-style illustration with light ink and watercolor washes showing a dark, gloomy landscape. Under a heavy grey sky, a series of bright red and orange flames or glowing ethereal lights emerge from the surface of the earth, following the slope of a hill.]

Master Zhu says:

When the virtuous are eliminated and "small men" <note>original: "小人" (xiaoren). This refers to people of low moral character or corrupt officials who seek personal gain over the public good.</note> are employed in government, then strange lights will arise from the earth.

The *Treatise of the Song* says:

When the earth suddenly produces light like fire that illuminates the capital, there is reason to worry about peril and ruin. Furthermore, it signifies that "small men" are being promoted while the virtuous are being destroyed.

<summary>This page discusses two specific omens—ice-covered trees (freezing rain) and eerie lights emerging from the ground—interpreting them as warnings of ministerial rebellion, the death of royalty, or the dominance of corrupt officials.</summary>

# Divination of Lightning Falling like Rain

[Image: A landscape painting depicts a dramatic storm. Swirling, dark grey ink washes in the upper right corner represent heavy clouds, from which long, diagonal, parallel brushstrokes in grey and blue descend across the scene, symbolizing torrential rain or lightning. Below, rounded, brownish hills are visible, with small, windswept trees clinging to the slopes, suggesting the power of the natural elements.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the influential Neo-Confucian scholar who synthesized natural phenomena with moral philosophy.</note> says:

When lightning falls like rain, or when lightning persists after the rain has cleared, it signifies that foreign tribes <note>original: "夷狄" (Yidi). A historical term for non-Han peoples on the borders of the Chinese empire, often translated as "barbarians."</note> will invade and insult the realm, and that ministers or the empress will monopolize power.

The *Treatise of the Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Referring to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" in the *History of the Song Dynasty*.</note> says:

When the sky "rains" lightning, it means that *Yin* is overpowering *Yang*. Generally, when *Yang* is prosperous, it results in rain. If *Yin* <term>Yin: (陰) the principle of darkness and femininity; here representing the "shadow" elements of the court, such as scheming officials or the empress’s kin.</term> pressures it, the rain turns into lightning because the energy is being coerced.

Ban Gu’s *Book of Han* <note>Ban Gu (32–92 AD) was the principal author of this foundational history of the Western Han Dynasty.</note> says:

Lightning is the result of *Yin* coercing *Yang*. It occurs because of an administration that acts through coercion and the monopolization of power.

<column-break/>

# Divination of the Shifting Mountains

[Image: A landscape painting illustrating mountain peaks in ink and light color. On the right, a large, craggy mountain massif rises with green-tinged peaks. To the left, a smaller, upright rock formation stands somewhat isolated on a flatter plane, with other smaller hills in the distance. This visual arrangement illustrates "山徒" (shifting mountains), a phenomenon regarded as a dire omen. Sparse, dark trees are scattered throughout the rocky terrain.]

Master Zhu says:

When mountains shift <note>original: "山徒" (Shantu). Literally "mountain walking" or "mountain migration," referring to landslides or the perceived movement of peaks.</note>, the Altars of Soil and Grain <term>Altars of Soil and Grain: (社稷) a metonym for the state or the ruling dynasty itself.</term> will perish.

The *Treatise of the Song* says:

When mountains move or shift, it is called "The Sovereign Failing to Establish the Ultimate." <note>original: "皇之不極" (Huang zhi bu ji). A classic omen category from the *Book of Documents* implying the ruler has failed to provide a moral or legal standard for the people.</note> Wealth departs from the public ducal house, and rewards and punishments issue from the "private gates" <note>Referring to powerful aristocratic families or factions operating outside the emperor's direct control.</note>. Conflict and war will break out throughout the world.

The "Metal Bound Casket" chapter of the *Classic of History* <note>original: "尚書金滕" (Shangshu Jinteng). A venerable text detailing the deeds of the Duke of Zhou.</note> says:

The shifting of mountains occurs when the ruler does not follow the Way. Wealth is lost, and the power to reward or punish no longer resides with the sovereign. Private factions form groups; this is known as "The Sovereign Failing to Establish the Ultimate."

<summary>This page describes the omens of lightning-storms and "shifting mountains," interpreting them as signs that the ruler has lost control to private factions, the empress, or foreign invaders.</summary>
<keywords>lightning, shifting mountains, Zhu Xi, Book of Han, Classic of History, Yin and Yang, political corruption, omens</keywords>

# Divination of Mountain Collapses and Surging Waters

[Image: A traditional Chinese ink and wash painting depicting a natural disaster. On the left, powerful, stylized waves with white-capped crests suggest a flood or rushing water. On the right, a rocky mountainside with a gnarled pine tree stands against the turbulent water, illustrating the theme of mountain collapse leading to surging waters.]

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晉書" (Jin Shu). The official history of the Jin Dynasty (266–420 AD), compiled in the 7th century, which includes detailed records of omens.</note> says:

The mountain represents the ruler <note>original: "君" (Jun). The sovereign or lord.</note>, who embodies the *Yang* <term>Yang: (陽) the principle of light, strength, and masculinity; in political cosmology, it represents the ruler.</term> principle. The water represents the common people <note>original: "百姓" (Baixing). Literally "the hundred surnames."</note>, who embody the *Yin* <term>Yin: (陰) the principle of darkness, receptivity, and femininity; here representing the subjects of the empire.</term> principle. This warning from Heaven is as if to say: the "Way of the Ruler" has collapsed and decayed, and the common people are about to lose their place of safety. Therefore, the mountains collapse or shift their positions, and the waters surge forth.

<column-break/>

# Divination of Mountain Collapses

[Image: A traditional Chinese ink and wash painting showing a mountain landslide. Several large boulders are depicted falling from a jagged cliff on the left side of the frame. To the right, the landscape settles into more distant, rounded green and grey hills with sparse vegetation and small trees.]

Master Zhu <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). Referring to the philosopher Zhu Xi.</note> says:

When a mountain collapses, the "Way of the Ruler" is ruined.

The *Treatise of the Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Referring to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" in the *History of the Song Dynasty*.</note> says:

When mountains collapse or are destroyed, it is called "the Excess of *Yang* and the Weakness of *Yin*." <note>This suggests an imbalance where the ruler's power is uncontrolled or brittle.</note> A collapse is a sign of dispersal and separation; it means that worthy men are departing the court while flatterers <note>original: "佞人" (Ningren). Corrupt officials who use smooth talk to gain favor.</note> are entering it.

The *Book of Jin* says:

When lesser men strip away the foundations <note>original: "小人剥盧" (Xiaoren baolu). This refers to the "Po" hexagram in the I Ching, symbolizing the "peeling away" or undermining of the structure of the state by corrupt individuals.</note>, the resulting anomaly is a mountain collapse. This is called "the Excess of *Yin* and the Weakness of *Yang*," where the weak overcome the strong. <note>Note the different interpretive tradition here, where the collapse is seen as the "Yin" elements—the corrupt subordinates—finally destroying the "Yang" structure of the state.</note>

<summary>This page explains how mountain landslides and floods are divine warnings of political instability, specifically symbolizing the collapse of a ruler's authority and the displacement of the people. It cites historical texts to show how these disasters mirror the departure of virtuous officials and the rise of corrupt flatterers at court.</summary>

# Divination of a Rain of Hair

[Image: A colored landscape illustration showing mountains and trees under a grey sky. Fine, dark strands representing a rain of hair or fur fall diagonally across the scene. A tall green rock formation stands prominently on a cliff to the right.]

---

Lord Zhu Wengong <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). This is the posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), one of the most influential philosophers in Chinese history, whose commentaries became the basis for the imperial examinations.</note> says:

When it rains hair, then military service and forced labor <term>徭: (yao) corvée labor, a system where the state conscripted commoners for unpaid labor on public works like roads, walls, or canals.</term> will continue without end.

The *Annals of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Likely referring to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the official *History of Song*, which catalogs omens and their outcomes.</note> says:

When the heavens rain hair, the fur-bearing creatures will lose their natural instincts. Within the state, the sycophants <note>original: "邦佞" (bangning). Corrupt officials who use flattery to gain influence.</note> will advance in rank while the virtuous men retreat; noblemen will be forced to flee into exile.

The *Book of Sui* <note>original: "隋書" (Sui Shu). The official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618 AD), compiled during the Tang Dynasty.</note> says:

When the heavens rain hair, public labor projects will flourish excessively, and forced conscription for war will never cease.

# Divination of a Rain of Feathers

[Image: A colored illustration of a landscape with a dark rocky hill on the left. Large, grey feathers fall from the sky in a diagonal rain-like pattern.]

Lord Zhu Wengong says:

When it rains feathers, then the value of the people will become lowly <note>This suggests that human life will be treated as cheap or that social status will be degraded.</note>.

The *Annals of Song* says:

When the heavens rain feathers, the ruler's virtue is unprincipled, acting in opposition to the natural order of the world.

Jing Fang <note>original: "京房" (77–37 BC). A Han dynasty scholar and astronomer who developed a sophisticated system linking natural disasters and weather patterns to the moral conduct of the Emperor.</note> says:

# Divination of a Rain of Golden Insects

[Image: An ink-wash landscape painting depicting green and grey mountains. The sky is filled with falling, colorful star-shaped or insect-like particles in red, yellow, orange, and green, illustrating the omen of "raining golden insects."]

Lord Zhu Wengong <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian philosopher whose interpretations of the classics were the standard for the imperial bureaucracy.</note> says:

A rain of golden insects <term>金蜞: (jinqi) Literally "golden leeches" or "golden insects." In historical omenology, these were often described as small, brightly colored creatures falling from the sky, symbolizing the "parasitic" nature of a corrupt state.</term> signifies greedy and oppressive governance.

The *Annals of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). This refers to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *History of Song*, which records anomalies and their political consequences.</note> says:

When the heavens rain golden insects, then kinfolk <note>original: "骨肉" (gurou). Literally "bone and flesh," meaning immediate family and close relatives.</note> will become estranged from one another, and the government will be tyrannical.

The *Spring and Autumn Annals Commentary* <note>original: "春秋傳" (Chunqiu Zhuan). Likely referring to one of the traditional commentaries (Zuo, Gongyang, or Guliang) on the ancient *Spring and Autumn Annals*.</note> says:

When the heavens rain golden insects, judicial punishments will be cruel and tyrannical, and predatory taxation <term>賊歛: (zeilian) Literally "thieving collection," referring to the state or officials seizing property and wealth from the people through extra-legal or excessive means.</term> will continue without end.

# Divination of a Rain of Gold and Iron

[Image: An ink-wash landscape painting of mountains under a grey sky. Numerous greyish and brownish flat shards or flakes fall from the sky, representing the omen of "raining gold and iron."]

Lord Zhu Wengong says:

A rain of gold and iron is the sign of a cruel regime.

When the heavens rain gold and iron, it is a sign of legal persecution <note>original: "刑獄" (xingyu). Literally "punishments and prisons," referring to a state of constant litigation or the weaponization of the law.</note> and it portends the disasters of war.

The *Book of Sui* <note>original: "隋書" (Sui Shu). The official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618 AD), which collapsed due to massive labor projects and failed military campaigns.</note> says:

# Divination of a Rain of Flesh

[Image: A woodblock-style illustration depicting a mountainous landscape under a pale sky. From a large, horizontal red cloud, several irregular red fragments representing "meat" fall toward the rocky terrain below.]

Lord Zhu Wengong <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of the famous scholar Zhu Xi (1130–1200), whose interpretations of natural phenomena were highly influential in imperial China.</note> says:

When it rains flesh, it signifies that the ruler does not cultivate his virtue.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* <note>original: "開元占" (Kaiyuan Zhan). This refers to the *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, a massive encyclopedia of astrology and omens compiled during the Tang Dynasty.</note> says:

If a ruler acts with violence and cruelty, the world will no longer benefit from his virtue, and the ruler will be replaced.

Xun Yue’s *History of Han* <note>original: "荀悦漢書" (Xun Yue Hanshu). Xun Yue (148–209 AD) was a scholar-official who compiled the *Hanji*, a chronological history of the Western Han dynasty.</note> says:

When the ruler's vision is clouded <note>original: "視之不明" (shi zhi bu ming). This refers to the Han-era "Five Elements" theory, where a ruler’s specific personal failings—in this case, poor judgment or lack of insight—trigger corresponding disasters in nature.</note>, it is called a lack of wisdom; then heaven rains flesh.

# Divination of a Rain of Blood

[Image: A woodblock-style illustration of a landscape with jagged green and grey mountains. The sky is filled with numerous red, teardrop-shaped droplets representing "blood" raining over the hills.]

Lord Zhu Wengong says:

When it rains blood, it signifies that the ruler is not close to his people.

The *Annals of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Specifically the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the official *History of Song*, which catalogs bizarre natural events as political omens.</note> says:

A rain of blood is a sign of an omen revealed by Heaven. Those who are unworthy shall not long occupy their positions of power, and within the year, war will arise <term>兵起: (bingqi) Literally "weapons arise," meaning the outbreak of military conflict or rebellion.</term>.

Ban Gu’s *History of Han* <note>original: "班固漢書" (Ban Gu Hanshu). The primary historical record of the Western Han Dynasty, written in the 1st century AD.</note> says:

If a rain of blood does not stop, the unworthy shall not be permitted to remain in their positions, and within the year, war will arise.

# Divination of a Rain of Ink

Lord Zhu Wengong <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi (1130–1200).</note> says:

When there are many secret conspiracies <note>original: "多陰謀" (duo yin mou). This refers to clandestine plots or intrigues within the imperial court or government.</note>, heaven will rain like ink.

The *History of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Likely referring to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *History of Song*, which records celestial and weather-based omens.</note> says:

When heaven rains black, there are many secret conspiracies.

# Divination of a Rain of Ash

[Image: A landscape showing mountain peaks shrouded in thick gray mist and clouds. Elongated gray particles representing ash fall from the top of the frame down through the valley.]

Lord Zhu Wengong says:

When there is tyrannical government <note>original: "暴政" (bao zheng). Despotic or oppressive rule that violates the Mandate of Heaven.</note>, heaven will rain ash.

The *History of Song* says:

A rain of ash is caused by tyranny. When the punitive campaign against the immoral King of Yin <note>original: "殷討無道" (Yin tao wu dao). This refers to the historical overthrow of the last king of the Shang (Yin) dynasty, who was considered a legendary tyrant, by the virtuous King Wu of Zhou.</note> took place, it rained heavily with ash.

The *Book of Sui* <note>original: "隋書" (Sui Shu). The official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618 AD), compiled during the Tang Dynasty.</note> says:

Heaven rains ash when the Emperor resents those whose talents surpass his own.

**Key Terms**

*   <term>Lord Zhu Wengong (朱文公)</term>: Posthumous title of Zhu Xi, a preeminent scholar whose commentaries became the basis for the imperial examination system.
*   <term>History of Song (宋志)</term>: A reference to the official dynastic records of the Song Dynasty (960–1279).
*   <term>Book of Sui (隋書)</term>: The historical record of the Sui Dynasty, often citing omens to explain the dynasty's fall.
*   <term>Tyranny (暴政)</term>: Harsh, oppressive rule that disturbs the natural harmony of the world.
*   <term>Conspiracies (陰謀)</term>: Hidden, malevolent plans that signify a lack of transparency in the state.
*   <term>Heavenly Rain (天雨)</term>: Weather events interpreted as direct messages or warnings from the divine sky.
*   <term>Rain of Ink (天雨如墨)</term>: A dark rain symbolizing the "darkened" or obscured intentions of officials.
*   <term>Rain of Ash (天雨成灰)</term>: Falling gray debris symbolizing a regime that has "burnt out" its moral authority.
*   <term>Punishing the Immoral Yin (殷討無道)</term>: A classic historical example used to show that natural disasters precede or accompany the removal of a bad ruler.

# Divination of a Rain of Golden Bowls

[Image: A woodblock-style illustration of a coastal landscape with a high, layered cliff on the left and a central rocky islet with pine trees. Numerous small red coin-like or petal-like objects are shown falling from dark clouds in the sky onto the scene.]

Lord Zhu Wengong <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi (1130–1200).</note> says:

A rain of golden bowls <note>original: "金甌" (jin ou). While literally "golden bowls," in historical records this often refers to specific fungal growths or small, round geological or botanical objects that appear after heavy rain, traditionally viewed as a supernatural sign of grain.</note> is a sign of a bountiful harvest year.

The *History of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Referring to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" in the official dynastic history of the Song.</note> says:

When objects the size of small coins emerge from the earth, and inside them are grains as large as millet, they are named "Golden Bowls." They signify a bountiful harvest. It is also said: if heaven rains golden bowls and yet people resort to cannibalism, it is because the "bowls" are empty inside <note>meaning the omen appeared, but the substance—the grain—was missing, indicating a false promise of plenty.</note>.

<column-break/>

# Divination of Heaven Descending "Ale-Cup Tin"

[Image: A woodblock-style illustration of sharp, jagged mountain peaks partially obscured by mist. Pale yellow streaks descend from dark, swirling clouds at the top of the frame onto the mountain peaks below.]

Lord Zhu Wengong says:

The descent of "Ale-Cup Tin" <note>original: "爵錫" (jue xi). A term for yellow-colored precipitation or deposits. "Jue" is a three-legged ritual wine vessel, and "Xi" means tin or a bright metal. This likely refers to yellow rain or pollen deposits that resemble the color of cast bronze or tin alloys.</note> is an anomaly indicating a change of ruler.

The *History of Song* says:

When heaven rains dew and one sees that objects have turned a yellow color, this is named "Ale-Cup Tin." Within three years, there will be a great uprising among the people, and it is said: "Below, there shall be a change."

The *Divination of the Yisi Year* <note>original: "乙巳占" (Yi Si Zhan). A famous 7th-century treatise on astrology and omens by the mathematician and astronomer Li Chunfeng.</note> says:

Within three years, the government will be reformed and the ruler will be replaced <note>original: "改政易主" (gai zheng yi zhu). This indicates a fundamental shift in the mandate to rule, often through revolution or succession crises.</note>.

<note>Vocabulary from the original text:
- Rain of Golden Bowls (天雨金甌): A rare phenomenon where small, bowl-like objects appear.
- Bountiful Harvest (歲穣): A year of plenty.
- Ale-Cup Tin (爵錫): A yellow atmospheric deposit.
- Change of Ruler (易主): The replacement of the sovereign.
- Reform of Government (改政): A change in political administration.</note>

<summary>This page describes two rare types of precipitation: "Golden Bowls," which typically portend agricultural abundance, and "Ale-Cup Tin" (yellow rain), which serves as a dire warning of impending political upheaval and the replacement of the monarch.</summary>

# Divination of Heaven Raining Ice

If it rains ice, then in that region <note>original: "分" (fen). Referring to a specific geographic area or its corresponding celestial division.</note> there will be a great plague.

The *History of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Referring to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" in the official dynastic history of the Song, which records natural disasters as political omens.</note> says:

When heaven rains ice, it means the element of water has lost its true nature; <note>In the "Five Elements" theory, water is supposed to flow and nourish. Transforming into ice out of season signifies a disruption in the cosmic balance (Yin and Yang).</note> therefore, in that region, there will be a great plague.

Ban Gu’s <note>original: "班固" (Ban Gu). A primary historian of the Eastern Han Dynasty (32–92 AD).</note> *Book of Han* <note>original: "漢書" (Han Shu). The classic history of the Western Han dynasty.</note> says:

# Divination of Thunder Occurring Out of Season
# Divination of Heaven Raining Without Clouds

[Image: An illustration of jagged green and grey mountain peaks beneath a large, dark, swirling storm cloud. Inside the cloud, three barrel-shaped drums are linked vertically, a traditional symbolic depiction of thunder.]

Lord Zhu Wengong <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian scholar whose interpretations of the classics and natural phenomena became state orthodoxy.</note> says:

When thunder sounds out of its proper season, <note>In the traditional Chinese calendar, thunder was expected to begin in the spring (the "Awakening of Insects") and cease in the autumn. Thunder in winter was seen as a major disruption of the natural order.</note> treacherous ministers are about to rise up.

The *History of Song* <note>original: "宋志" (Song Zhi). Referring to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the official dynastic history.</note> says:

If thunder breaks out when it is not the correct time, high-ranking ministers will monopolize the administration and the Empress <note>original: "女后" (nü hou). Referring to the Empress or Empress Dowager exercising power from "behind the curtain."</note> will seize authority.

The *Book of Jin* <note>original: "晉書" (Jin Shu). The official history of the Jin Dynasty (266–420 AD).</note> says:

Thunder out of season occurs because the sovereign has lost the correct way of governance; treacherous ministers will arise.

<column-break/>

[Image: A landscape with several mountain peaks and sparse trees. Thin, vertical lines representing rain fall from a pale, relatively clear sky that lacks dense storm clouds.]

Lord Zhu Wengong says:

Rain falling without clouds means that enfeoffments and appointments <note>original: "封拜" (feng bai). The granting of noble titles and high offices.</note> are being granted to those who have no merit.

The *History of Song* says:

Rain without clouds is a sign of "irreverence in demeanor." <note>original: "貌之不恭" (mao zhi bu gong). One of the "Five Matters" from the *Book of Documents*. Traditional Chinese political theory held that if the ruler's physical bearing was not respectful and grave, the cosmos would respond with erratic weather.</note> This is called "failing to reflect" on one's errors; consequently, disaster and misfortune will bring total destruction.

The *Book of Sui* <note>original: "隋書" (Sui Shu). The official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618 AD).</note> says:

When heaven rains without clouds, it signifies that rebellious ministers have been executed. <note>Unlike the other omens on this page, the *Book of Sui* interprets this specific anomaly as a positive sign of the restoration of order through the punishment of traitors.</note>

# Divination of Heaven Raining Yellow Sand
# Divination of Frost Falling During the Day

[Image: The left panel contains an illustration of a landscape with green, rolling hills and stylized trees. Above the horizon, the sky is filled with thick, swirling clouds tinted with yellow and grey, depicting a "rain of yellow sand."]

Lord Zhu Wengong <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher whose writings often linked natural phenomena to the morality of the government.</note> says:

When heaven rains yellow sand, <note>This likely refers to severe dust storms originating from the Gobi Desert, which can turn the sky yellow and deposit thick layers of silt. In divination, this was seen as a disturbance of the Earth element.</note> rebellious troops will rise up below.

[Image: The right panel contains an illustration of a rocky landscape with sharp peaks and sparse vegetation. The sky is rendered with pale horizontal bands, representing the cold atmosphere of a daytime frost.]

Lord Zhu Wengong says:

If the falling of frost and snow is not at its proper time, the administration of the state lies with the high ministers and not with the sovereign. <note>original: "不在群" (bu zai qun). Literally "not with the group/assembly," here referring to the loss of centralized authority to powerful individual officials or cliques.</note>

The *Book of Northern Qi* <note>original: "北齊書" (Beiqi Shu). The official dynastic history of the Northern Qi (550–577 AD).</note> says:

When frost falls during the day, the ruler will pass authority to the Crown Prince. <note>This implies an early or forced abdication, as frost during the day—when the sun should be strongest—symbolizes the "Yin" (the heir) overshadowing the "Yang" (the ruler).</note>

The *Book of Liang* <note>original: "梁書" (Liang Shu). The official dynastic history of the Liang Dynasty (502–557 AD).</note> says:

When frost falls in the sixth month, <note>The sixth lunar month falls in mid-summer. Frost at this time would be an agricultural disaster.</note> the common people will suffer from toil and famine.

# Divination of Constant Rain

[Image: A traditional ink and wash painting depicting a landscape during a heavy rainstorm. Strong, dark diagonal brushstrokes represent sheets of rain falling from a dark, grey sky. In the lower left, a lone figure wearing a conical rain hat and traditional robes walks through the downpour. On the right, a gnarled, leafy tree grows from a rocky slope. In the background, the faint outlines of distant mountains are visible through the mist.]

The *Book of the Later Han* by Fan Ye <note>original: "范曄漢書" (Fan Ye Hanshu). Fan Ye (398–445 AD) was the compiler of this official history. While the text says "Han Shu," it refers specifically to his history of the Eastern/Later Han period.</note> says:

Wood <note>In the Five Elements (Wuxing) system, "Wood" corresponds to spring, growth, and the color green.</note> governs the *qi* <term>Qi: The vital energy or life force that circulates through the universe and the human body.</term> of spring and the power of life-generation. When this life-generating energy is lost or corrupted, nature oversteps its proper seasonal rhythms; for this reason, it rains constantly.

# Divination of Constant Overcast

[Image: A traditional ink and wash painting of a landscape under an overcast sky. The upper half of the frame is filled with a heavy, uniform grey wash indicating thick cloud cover. On the left, tall, jagged mountain peaks are rendered with dark ink and light green coloration. To the right, the terrain transitions into softer, brownish hills. Several dark, sparse trees are scattered across the middle ground, creating a somber, quiet atmosphere.]

The *Book of the Later Han* by Fan Ye says:

The sovereign’s ultimate character is reflected in the colors of the sky. ### ->Divination of the Ill-Omened Sun Emerging at Night; Divination of Meteoric Flows Encroaching upon the Sun<-

<image-desc>A landscape painting of dark, craggy mountains or islands set in water against a grey-blue sky. In the upper center, a single large red sun is encircled by a faint, diffuse halo.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of the philosopher Zhu Xi. His inclusion here suggests these omens were taken seriously by the intellectual elite.</note> says:
If an ill-omened sun emerges at night, the <term>Social Order: "紀綱" (jìgāng). This term literally refers to the "ropes of a net," symbolizing the laws, morals, and discipline that keep a civilization from unraveling.</term> is utterly destroyed.

**The *Treatise of Song*** says:
When the sun appears at night, it is called <term>Yin Radiance: "陰明" (yīnmíng). A paradoxical term suggesting that the dark, passive force (Yin) has improperly usurped the light of the sun.</term> It signifies that war will break out throughout the realm. Subordinates will rebel against their superiors, and great floods will spread. If the sun and moon are seen together at night, the realm will be divided.

**The *Metal Coffer* chapter of the *Book of Documents*** <note>original: "尚書金縢" (Shàngshū Jīnténg). An ancient text concerning the divine right to rule.</note> says:
When the sun appears at night, the social order is destroyed, high ministers will monopolize the government, and the ruler's sovereign authority will be stripped away.

**The *Kaiyuan Divination*** <note>original: "開元占" (Kāiyuán Zhàn). A massive Tang dynasty encyclopedia of astrology and omens.</note> says:

**Master Zhu Wengong** says:
When <term>Flying Flows: "飛流" (fēiliú). Bright, moving celestial objects such as meteors, bolides, or comets that appear to move toward or "attack" the sun.</term> encroach upon the sun, the administration will be forced to change, the people will become wandering refugees and suffer from disease, and the King will pass away.

**The *Treatise of Song*** says:
When flying flows encroach upon the sun, reflecting against its light and appearing sharp at the front and square at the rear, disaster will reach the palaces of the ministers. There will be unrest, and the world will tremble. If the sun loses its light, the people will suffer from pestilence and death.
