### ->Divination of Multiple Suns Appearing Together; Divination of Darkness Occurring During the Day<-

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese ink and color landscape illustration within a double-line border. The sky features three red suns. The sun on the far right is the largest and is enveloped by a multi-layered circular halo in shades of light blue and red. The two other suns are smaller, solid red circles. Below the sky is a mountainous landscape rendered in grey and green washes with jagged, vertical peaks. A lone pine tree is perched on a rocky cliff to the left.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhu Wengong). The posthumous name of the influential philosopher Zhu Xi (1130–1200 CE), whose commentaries became the basis for the imperial examination system.</note> says:
When multiple suns appear together, it signifies that the realm will be divided and in conflict.

**The *Treatise of Song*** <note>original: "宋志" (Sòng Zhì). Likely referring to the "Treatise on Celestial Phenomena" within the *History of the Song Dynasty* (*Song Shi*).</note> says:
When two suns appear together, the realm will resort to weapons of war. Those who are <term>Without the Way: "無道" (wúdào). Rulers who have lost their moral right to govern and are out of harmony with the natural order.</term> shall perish. This is known as "Bright Yang," where a <term>False Ruler: "假主" (jiǎzhǔ). A pretender to the throne or a powerful subordinate who acts with the authority of the emperor.</term> challenges and contends for power. In such a case, the states below will fall into chaos. If three suns appear together, the trouble will last no more than thirty days. When feudal lords compete and multiple suns appear, the realm will be divided. If two armies are facing each other and several suns appear, there will be a great battle and cities will be seized; one should divide the military camps to respond to this omen.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese ink and color landscape illustration within a double-line border. In the sky, a single solid red sun is depicted. The sky has a slightly darker, murky wash compared to the previous image. The landscape below consists of craggy grey mountain peaks with green accents and several pine trees growing along the slopes and ridges.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** says:
When the sun is dark and obscured during the day, <term>Yin: "陰" (yīn). The feminine, dark, and passive principle.</term> has conversely become <term>Yang: "陽" (yáng). The masculine, bright, and active principle, traditionally associated with the Emperor.</term> This signifies that a minister or subordinate will control the ruler.

**The *Treatise of Song*** says:
If the day is dim and travelers cast no shadows, and if this continues until evening without stopping, it signifies that <term>Urgent Punishments: "刑急" (xíngjí). A state of political crisis where the government resorts to harsh, hurried, or excessive legal penalties.</term> are being imposed. If this occurs, there will be great floods within a year. When the day is dark, flocks of birds will fly in chaos, and the <term>Divided Territory: "分土" (fēntǔ). The fragmentation of the empire's land among warring factions or local lords.</term> will result.

<summary>This page describes the omens of multiple suns (parhelia) and midday darkness, interpreting them as celestial warnings of civil war, the rise of pretenders to the throne, and the loss of imperial control over ministers.</summary>
<keywords>parhelia, multiple suns, solar obscuration, Zhu Xi, Song Dynasty, civil war, usurpation, Yin and Yang, political omens</keywords>

### ->Divination of Sunspots Appearing Black<-

<image-desc>A landscape illustration depicting craggy mountains and trees under a pale sky. In the upper left, a large red sun contains five distinct, dark spots (sunspots) clustered in its center.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhū Wéngōng). The posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian scholar.</note> says:
If <term>Sunspots: "黑子" (hēizǐ). Literally "black seeds," referring to the dark spots visible on the sun’s surface.</term> appear with a black color,
sometimes numbering three and sometimes five, it means
ministers are plotting against the ruler, or the ministers are in revolt; it also signifies that <term>Ranks and Rewards: "爵賞" (juéshǎng). The system of nobility titles and material rewards used by the Emperor to maintain order and loyalty.</term> are being distributed unfairly.

**The Grand Duke** <note>original: "太公" (Tàigōng). Referring to Jiang Ziya, the legendary strategist and advisor to the founders of the Zhou Dynasty, often cited as an authority on omens and strategy.</note> says:
If within the sun there are <term>Black Vapors: "黑氣" (hēiqì). Atmospheric or solar phenomena described as dark streaks or smudges.</term> numbering 
one, two, three, four, or five, 
it means the government's instructions and orders are not clear; the <term>Three Ducal Ministers: "三公" (sāngōng). The three highest-ranking officials in the imperial government.</term> are causing chaos, and 
ranks and rewards are being distributed unfairly.

<column-break/>

### ->Divination of Black Vapor Within the Sun<-

<image-desc>A landscape illustration with towering blue and green mountains and sparse trees. In the upper right, a red sun is shown with a diffused, dark circular vapor or smudge in its center.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** says:
Black vapor within the sun means that ministers do not hide their evil deeds, and the 
common people loathe the ruler.

**The *Treatise of Song*** <note>original: "宋志" (Sòng Zhì). The astronomical and omen records within the History of the Song Dynasty.</note> says:
Black vapor within the sun symbolizes the intention of Heaven not being in harmony. 
Black vapor is also considered a <term>Veiling: "薄" (bó). An astronomical term for a light haze or obscuration that "assaults" or diminishes the sun's light.</term>; these are all manifestations of <term>Yin: "陰" (yīn). The dark, passive, or "subordinate" principle in nature, associated here with ministers or the common people overstepping their bounds.</term>. If 
they appear sometimes as three and sometimes as five, then ministers are plotting; others say 
it means the ministers are obscuring the ruler. This is caused by the lack of clarity 
resulting from the black vapor within the sun.

### ->Divination of the Sun and Moon Appearing Simultaneously<-

<image-desc>A rectangular framed illustration depicting two celestial bodies in a gray sky above a landscape of blue and green mountains. On the right is a red disc with a golden outline (the sun), and on the left is a pale yellow disc with a golden outline (the moon), shown appearing simultaneously.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhū Wéngōng). The posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian philosopher whose interpretations became the basis for the imperial examination system.</note> says:
When the sun and moon appear together, ministers will rebel and the <term>Barbarians: "夷狄" (yídí). A historical term used to refer to non-Han ethnic groups on the borders of China, often seen as a threat to the Central Kingdom.</term> will invade.

**The History of Song** <note>original: "宋志" (Sòng Zhì). Likely referring to the astronomical or "Five Elements" treatises within the *Song Shi* (History of the Song Dynasty).</note> says:
When the sun and moon appear together, the nation will be divided and war shall break out. If they are separated by only a few inches, ministers will rebel and plot against the sovereign. It also says: when the sun and moon shine together, if the sun's light is not strong but the moon's light alone is dominant, this indicates that the <term>Empress or Consorts: "后妃" (hòufēi). Referring to the women of the imperial palace.</term> are <term>Usurping Power: "擅權" (shànquán). Exercising authority without proper legal or moral right.</term> It also says: when the sun and moon are both seen during the daylight hours, war will arise and ministers will rebel. This occurred when the state of Yue destroyed the state of Wu <note>A famous historical conflict during the Spring and Autumn period (c. 5th century BCE).</note>; it signifies ministers deceiving their ruler and barbarians invading the Central Kingdom.

### ->Divination of "Teeth" and "Feet" Appearing Together<-

<image-desc>A rectangular framed illustration showing the sun as a red disc with a golden halo, partially surrounded by dark, claw-like clouds that extend downwards into long, jagged streaks (described in the text as "feet" or "teeth"). Below is a stylized landscape with green-peaked mountains and small trees.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** says:
When <term>"Teeth and Feet": "齒足" (chǐzú). Metaphorical terms for solar phenomena; "teeth" refer to jagged protrusions from the sun's disk, while "feet" refer to rays or streaks of light (crepuscular rays) stretching toward the horizon.</term> are both seen, the army will be defeated and the general will die.

**The History of Song** says:
When solar rays between the clouds reach the ground, they are called "feet." If they are red, there will be an uprising of troops; if they are white, there will be defeated generals and the ruin of the sovereign. If the sun has "teeth" and "feet," those below will rebel.

**The Apothegm of the Spring and Autumn Annals** <note>original: "春秋感精符" (Chūnqiū Gǎnjīng Fú). An ancient apocryphal text (weishu) that uses the "Spring and Autumn Annals" to interpret omens and the connection between heaven and humanity.</note> says:
When foreign wars and invasions occur simultaneously, and troops are deployed under a general, then "teeth" will emerge and "feet" will be raised from the sun.

### ->Divination of the Sun’s Yellow Color | Divination of the Sun Responding by Turning Red<-

<image-desc>A landscape painting featuring a pale grey sky with a yellow sun that has a thin red outer ring. Below the sun are various jagged mountain peaks in shades of blue-grey and green, with stylized green trees growing on the slopes.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhū Wéngōng). The posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), a famous philosopher whose work shaped the moral and political code of imperial China.</note> says:
If the sun turns yellow, it means the ruler hears of good and virtuous deeds but does not participate in them or support them.

**The History of Song** <note>original: "宋志" (Sòng Zhì). This refers to the "Treatise on the Five Elements" or the "Treatise on Astronomy" within the official dynastic history of the Song.</note> says:
When the color of the sun is yellow, the ruler hears of good deeds but does not join in them.

**Jing Fang** <note>original: "京房" (77–37 BC). A Han dynasty scholar and master of the *I Ching* who specialized in interpreting natural disasters and celestial omens as criticisms of government.</note> says:
When the words of a <term>Worthy: "賢者" (xiánzhě). A person of high moral character and talent.</term> are put into practice, yet the person themselves is obscured or sidelined; or when someone takes credit for another's excellence to boast of their own merit—then the color of the sun will surely be yellow.

<image-desc>A landscape painting showing a solid red sun in a pale sky. The ground below consists of dark, rounded hills or rocky mounds with sparse, leafless trees and small shrubs.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu Wengong** says:
If <term>Orders and Decrees: "號令" (hàolìng). Official commands issued by the emperor or government.</term> harm the people, the sun responds by turning red.

**The History of Song** says:
A red color in the sun indicates that the ruler lacks wisdom.

**Jing Fang** says:
When the issuing of orders and decrees repeatedly harms the common people, the sun responds by turning red.

<summary>This page explores the moral interpretation of solar color shifts, where a yellow sun signifies the ruler's failure to recognize virtue and a red sun warns of harmful government policies.</summary>

### Divination of Red Vapors Like a Pestle Striking the Sun, and Like Axes Beside the Sun

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese illustration of an astronomical omen. Against a backdrop of misty grey sky and jagged green mountains with dark trees, a bright red sun is depicted. ### Divination of a Curved Shape Facing Away from the Sun

<image-desc>An illustration of a red sun in a grey sky. Above the sun is a dark, ribbon-like cloud formation that curves away from the sun. Below is a landscape with dark rocky mountains and sparse vegetation.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhū Wéngōng). This refers to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian philosopher, whose work integrated cosmology with political ethics.</note> states:

When a shape curves away from the sun, it is called <term>Backing<gloss>original: "背" (bèi); this refers to an atmospheric arc that turns its back to the sun, symbolizing a rupture in the natural or political order.</gloss></term>. This signifies a minister rebelling or an act of treacherous disobedience.

**The Treatises of the Song** <note>original: "宋志" (Sòng Zhì). The astronomical records within the official History of the Song Dynasty.</note> state:

If a curved shape faces outward, it constitutes "Backing," which signifies betrayal. It is a sign of defiance; it also suggests that there are rebels among those in lower positions.

<column-break/>

### Divination of a Curved Shape Facing Toward the Sun

<image-desc>An illustration of a red sun in a grey sky. Beneath the sun is a yellow crescent-shaped cloud or atmospheric halo that curves around the bottom of the sun, as if embracing it. Below the sky is a landscape featuring steep grey cliffs and green pine trees.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** states:

A shape that curves toward the sun is called <term>Embracing<gloss>original: "抱" (bào); an atmospheric phenomenon where a halo or cloud appears to enfold the sun, symbolizing protection, intimacy, or loyalty.</gloss></term>. This signifies the joy of a son and the loyalty of a minister.

**The Treatises of the Song** state:

When a yellow <term>vapor<gloss>original: "氣" (qì); atmospheric emanations believed to be "breaths" of the cosmos that signal future events.</gloss></term> curves toward the sun, it is "Embracing." This means there shall be joy among children and grandchildren, loyalty among ministers, and neighboring countries shall come to offer their surrender.

**The Treatises of the Jin** <note>original: "晉志" (Jìn Zhì). The astronomical records from the official History of the Jin Dynasty (266–420 CE).</note> state:

If there is something like a half-ring beside the sun facing toward it, this is "Embracing."

**The Divination of the Yisi Year** <note>original: "乙巳占" (Yǐsì Zhàn). An influential astrological compendium written by the Tang Dynasty polymath Li Chunfeng (602–670 CE).</note> states:

If two armies are facing one another, this omen signifies a peaceful reconciliation.

## Divination of a Long and Vertical Shape called "Straight"

<image-desc>An ink and wash landscape painting depicting mountains and trees under a pale sky. In the sky, a red sun is shown with a single vertical red line positioned to its right, representing the "zhi" (straight) atmospheric phenomenon.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** <note>original: "朱文公" (Zhū Wéngōng). Referring to Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian scholar who interpreted natural omens as reflections of the Mandate of Heaven.</note> states:

That which is long and standing upright is called <term>Straight<gloss>original: "直" (zhí); a vertical pillar of light or vapor appearing beside the sun.</gloss></term>. This signifies that below, there is someone who will establish themselves independently. <note>This "self-establishment" usually implies a local leader or general declaring independence from the central imperial authority.</note>

**The Treatises of the Song** <note>original: "宋志" (Sòng Zhì). The astronomical records contained within the official *History of the Song Dynasty*.</note> state:

When a vertical vapor more than ten feet in length stands beside the sun, it is "Straight Vapor." This indicates that in the world below, there is one who establishes themselves independently.

**The Divinations of the Yisi Year** <note>original: "乙巳占" (Yǐsì Zhàn). A famous astrological compendium written by the Tang dynasty astronomer Li Chunfeng (602–670).</note> state:

In that specific region <note>In traditional Chinese astrology, the sky was divided into sections corresponding to specific terrestrial provinces.</note>, there will be a king who establishes himself.

## Divination of a Round and Small Shape called an "Ear"

<image-desc>An ink and wash landscape painting of mountain peaks and sparse trees. In the sky, a red sun is flanked on both sides by small, curved red marks resembling parentheses, representing solar "ears" (parhelia).</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** states:

That which is round and small is called an <term>Ear<gloss>original: "珥" (ěr); technically a parhelion or "sun dog," appearing as a bright spot or fragment of a halo on either side of the sun.</gloss></term>. Those upon whom this light shines will experience joy.

**The Treatises of the Song** state:

When the vapor is round and small and sits beside the sun, it is an "Ear." Those whom it overlooks will have cause for celebration.

**Wang Shuo** <note>A Han dynasty scholar whose commentaries often linked astronomy with the hierarchy of the imperial court.</note> states:

The term "Ear" refers to the physical ear. The "Ear" vapor represents the close ministers of the sovereign; they are the people most intimate with the ruler, and they ought to function just as ears do <note>Meaning they should listen faithfully and stay close to the "head" or ruler.</note>.

# Divination of a Single Ear Beside the Sun

# Divination of Five Ears Beside the Sun

(The illustration shows a red sun in a pale blue sky, surrounded by five red crescent-shaped "ears"—two on the left side and three on the right. Below is a landscape featuring a cluster of trees on a rocky shore to the left, a river, and a small wooden bridge on the right leading toward hills in the distance.)

Jing Fang <note>Jing Fang (78–37 BCE), a famous Han dynasty scholar and cosmologist known for his expertise in the *I Ching* and his theories on atmospheric omens</note> says:

If five ears appear around the sun in the morning, the state will suffer from the anxiety of warfare breaking out. If they appear in the evening, there will certainly be a "Great Guest" <note>original: 大客 (Dà Kè); a high-ranking foreign dignitary or a significant diplomatic envoy</note>.

# Divination of Omen Resembling Straight Rain Intersecting

# Divination of the Jue Omen, Shaped Like a Back with a Rising Center

(The illustration shows a landscape with a small thatched-roof boat on water near rocky, green-topped hills. In the sky, a solid red sun is topped by a red cloud formation that is horizontal with a distinct hump or peak in the center, resembling the shape of the Chinese character for "mountain.")

# Divination of the Sun with a Crown, Cord, and two Ear-rings

On the left and right sides of the sun are two sets of concentric red arcs representing <term>Ear-rings <note>original: er (珥); parhelia, commonly known as "sun dogs."</note></term>. Beneath the sun is a horizontal series of interlocking red loops representing a <term>Cord <note>original: niu (紐); a knotted or loop-like optical phenomenon appearing below the sun.</note></term>. The landscape below includes sharp, blue and green mountain peaks rising from a misty valley with pine trees.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:

Rebellion and treason are all eliminated when the Crown, the Cord, and the two Ear-rings appear.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* says:

When there is a Crown and a Cord with Ear-rings to the left and right, the world possesses virtuous people, and those who are rebellious are removed.

# Divination of the Sun with Two "Backs" and one "Straight" Line

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese illustration of a solar omen. A red sun is depicted in the sky with two red crescent-shaped arcs, one positioned above and one below the solar disk, curving away from it. To the right of the sun is a single vertical red line. Below this celestial scene is a landscape of craggy, jagged mountains and sparse, stylized trees.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher often cited in these texts.</note> says:

When there are <term>Two Backs <note>original: er bei (二背); arcs of light that curve away from the sun, resembling two backs turned toward each other.</note></term> and <term>One Straight line <note>original: yi zhi (一直); a vertical shaft of light, likely a sun pillar.</note></term>, a high official is plotting to establish himself as an independent ruler.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* <note>The *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, an 8th-century astrological compendium.</note> says:

If the sun has two "Backs" and one "Straight" line, it means a high official is plotting rebellion and wishes to establish their own independent rule.

# Divination of the Sun with "Embracing Ear-rings" and "Doubled Light"

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese illustration of a solar omen. This phenomenon is set above a scenic landscape featuring blue and green mountains with prominent pine trees.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:

Blessings and official prosperity will descend together when the <term>Embracing Ear-rings <note>original: bao er (抱珥); halos that appear to "clasp" or "hug" the sides of the sun like jewelry.</note></term> and <term>Doubled Light <note>original: chong guang (重光); an atmospheric effect where the sun appears to have multiple layers of brilliance or concentric circles.</note></term> are seen.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* says:

The "Embracing Ear-rings" and "Doubled Light" appear as a sign of good fortune; blessings and official prosperity shall descend together.

# Divination of the Sun with the "Crown" Vapor

<image-desc>A watercolor illustration of a solar omen. A solid red sun hangs in a pale sky, with a horizontal green bar (the "crown" or dai) floating directly above it. Below is a traditional ink-wash landscape featuring stylized green-sloped mountain peaks and sparse trees.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher whose commentaries were standard for imperial examinations.</note> says:

Know that when the sun has a <term>Crown <note>original: dai (戴); an atmospheric phenomenon where a horizontal arc of light sits atop the sun, resembling a headpiece.</note></term> or a "Cap," the Sovereign <note>The Emperor.</note> will have cause for celebration.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* <note>The *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, a massive astrological compendium compiled during the Tang Dynasty.</note> says:

If there is a "Crown" and its colors are distinct—yellow and white, appearing moist and lustrous—the Son of Heaven will have cause for celebration.

# Divination of the Sun with One "Embrace" and Two "Ear-rings"

<image-desc>A watercolor illustration of solar parhelia. A red sun is flanked on both sides by two sets of crescent arcs (the "earrings" or er) and a larger, multi-colored arc (the "embrace" or bao) curving over the top. The sun is positioned above a landscape of sharp, rocky mountain crags and trees rendered in ink and light color.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:

One <term>Embrace <note>original: bao (抱); an arc of light that curves toward the sun as if "hugging" it.</note></term> and two <term>Ear-rings <note>original: er (珥); also known as "sun dogs" or parhelia, these appear as points or arcs of light on either side of the sun.</note></term> mean the Sovereign will have cause for celebration, and this state of joy shall be lasting.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* says:

One "Embrace" and two "Ear-rings" mean the Crown Prince will have cause for celebration.

If there is a yellow vapor below the sun shaped like a crescent moon, the Crown Prince will have cause for celebration.

## Divination of the Sun with a Crown-Cap Above and a Knot Below

<image-desc>A painting depicting a solar omen. In the upper sky, the sun is represented as a solid red disk. Above the sun is a single curved orange-red arc resembling a cap (冠). Below the sun is a chain of four interlocking red loops representing a knot (紐). Below the sky is a landscape of sharp, blue-and-black craggy mountain peaks.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the renowned Neo-Confucian scholar whose work often integrated natural philosophy with moral governance.</note> says:

If the Sovereign <note>The Emperor.</note> is personally intimate with <term>treacherous officials <note>original: jianchen (姦臣); corrupt or manipulative ministers who lead the ruler astray.</note></term>, the sun will display a <term>Crown-Cap <note>original: guan (冠); a curved solar halo appearing directly above the sun like a hat.</note></term> and a <term>Knot <note>original: niu (紐); a rare atmospheric phenomenon where loops of light appear to interlock beneath the solar disk.</note></term>.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* <note>The *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, an 8th-century astrological compendium.</note> says:

A "Crown and Knot" indicates that the Sovereign is observing women and engaging in private, illicit relations. It further says: This is a sign that the Sovereign wishes to establish a <term>woman of low-birth <note>original: qingyi (青衣); literally "green-clad," a term for domestic servants or those of low social status.</note></term> as his primary wife.

## Divination of the Sun with "Ear-rings" and a "Crown-Arc"

<image-desc>A painting depicting a solar omen. In the upper sky, the sun is a solid red disk. Above the sun is a single horizontal arc (戴). The *Kaiyuan Divination* says:

When there are "Ear-rings" and a "Crown-Arc," the Master of Men <note>The Emperor.</note> will have cause for joy, and the world will enjoy peace and harmony.

### Divination of the Sun with a Fringe and Ear-rings

<image-desc>An illustration of an atmospheric solar phenomenon. The sun is represented as a solid red circle. Above it is a "crown" (冠) consisting of four red arcs of increasing width stacked vertically. Flanking the sun are two red arcs representing "ears" (珥). Below the sun is a landscape scene featuring a small pavilion with a blue roof nestled among rocky hills and trees.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher whose commentaries often linked natural events to the moral conduct of the state.</note> says:

When a <term>Crown <note>original: guan (冠); a solar halo arc appearing directly above the sun.</note></term> and <term>Ear-rings <note>original: er (珥); parhelia or "sun dogs" appearing as arcs or spots on the left and right of the sun.</note></term> appear, and <term>Back-to-Back Rings <note>original: beijue (背玦); atmospheric arcs that resemble the "jue" jade ring with a gap, positioned back-to-back.</note></term> move confusedly among them, it signifies that the ruler will bring disorder to the nation.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* <note>The *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, a massive 8th-century encyclopedia of Chinese astrology and omens.</note> says:

If the sun displays Back-to-Back Rings while a Crown and Ear-rings are present, and the vapors are mixed and chaotic within the display, the ruler will bring disorder to the state, and the <term>Son of Heaven <note>The Emperor.</note></term> will be burdened with worry.

Master Zhu says:

When the <term>Inner Palace <note>original: hougong (後宮); the residence of the empress and imperial consorts.</note></term> is about to have a joyful event, then the sun will display Ear-rings and a <term>Fringe <note>original: ying (纓); a curved halo appearing beneath the sun, resembling the tassels or chin-straps of a ceremonial hat.</note></term>.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* says:

A Fringe accompanied by Ear-rings indicates that the Inner Palace has cause for joy.

### Divination of the Sun with Embracing Vapors
### Divination of the Sun with the Four Straights and Back-Rings

<image-desc>A traditional ink wash landscape painting of craggy mountains and sparse trees. In the sky, a large red sun is centered between two symmetrical sets of multi-colored arcs: the inner arcs are reddish-brown and the outer ones are light green. This illustrates the "baoqi" (embracing vapors) atmospheric phenomenon.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the renowned Neo-Confucian scholar.</note> says:

> When there are many <term>Embraces <note>original: bao (抱); solar halo arcs that curve inward, appearing to "hug" the sun.</note></term> and few <term>Straights <note>original: zhi (直); vertical pillars or streaks of light.</note></term>, those who wish to establish themselves independently will meet with no success.

The *Treatises of Song* <note>Likely referring to the astronomical treatises in the *Song Shi* (History of Song).</note> say:

> Embraces are <term>Compliant Vapors <note>original: shunqi (順氣); atmospheric signs indicating harmony with the natural or political order.</note></term>. If there are many Embraces and few Straights, those planning for the state will fail to establish their aims. If two armies are facing each other and miscellaneous vapors appear beside the sun, those with "Embraces" should be sent to attack. Those without "Embraces" should fight in accordance with the direction of the <term>Rainbow <note>original: hong (虹); here referring to a specific atmospheric arc used for orientation in battle.</note></term>.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A traditional ink wash landscape painting showing jagged mountain peaks and trees. Above the landscape, a red sun is depicted with several cinnabar-red atmospheric markers: a horizontal inverted arc (the "back-ring") directly above the sun and two pairs of vertical lines (the "four straights") on either side.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:

> When <term>Back-Rings <note>original: beijue (背玦); arcs that curve away from the sun, resembling the shape of a 'jue' (a jade ring with a gap).</note></term> and the <term>Four Straights <note>original: sizhi (四直); four vertical pillars of light.</note></term> intersect within, it means palace officials desire to act perversely. If the Straights are few and the Back-Rings are many, it is certain that those seeking to establish themselves independently will emerge.

The *Kaiyuan Divination* <note>The *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, an 8th-century astrological compendium.</note> says:

> If the sun has Back-Rings and the Four Straights intersect in the center, ministers are acting perversely.

The *Treatises of Song* say:

> Back-Rings are <term>Rebellious Vapors <note>original: niqi (逆氣); atmospheric signs indicating opposition, betrayal, or chaos.</note></term>. If there are few Back-Rings and many Straights, those planning for the state will surely succeed.

<summary>This page describes how different configurations of solar halos—specifically "Embracing Vapors" and "Back-Rings"—serve as omens for political stability or rebellion. Arcs curving toward the sun are seen as compliant and favorable for the state, while those curving away indicate treachery by ministers.</summary>
<keywords>solar halos, omens, atmospheric phenomena, Zhu Xi, military strategy, rebellion, Compliant Vapors, Rebellious Vapors, parhelia</keywords>

### Divination of the Sun with a Black Halo

<image-desc>A watercolor painting depicting a red sun surrounded by a thick, dark, hazy black halo in a grey sky. Below the celestial phenomenon is a landscape with two dark green rocky peaks on the left and a larger, layered rocky cliff on the right with sparse pine trees. A single figure in a long robe stands on the right cliff, looking towards the sun.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian philosopher of the Song Dynasty, who also wrote on natural phenomena.</note> says:
> If the color is black, then the grain crops will be harmed by great floods.

The *Divinations of the Kaiyuan Era* <note>original: Kaiyuan Zhan (開元占); referring to the *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, a massive astrological compendium compiled during the Tang Dynasty (714–724 CE).</note> say:
> A sun with a <term>Black Halo <note>original: heiyun (黑暈); a dark atmospheric ring around the sun, viewed as a highly negative omen.</note></term> signifies that disaster will befall the ministers currently in power.

<column-break/>

### Divination of a Solar Halo with Embracing Ear-rings and Carrying Vapors

<image-desc>A watercolor painting showing a red sun accompanied by complex atmospheric phenomena: multi-colored arcs of red and green (parhelia or "sun dogs" and halos) flanking it. Below, a landscape features a simple open-sided pavilion on the left, jagged rocks, and several pine trees clinging to the slopes.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:
> In times of peace, many <term>Solar Halos <note>original: riyun (日暈); general term for rings or arcs around the sun caused by ice crystals.</note></term> primarily signify wind and rain. However, when facing an enemy, a solar halo signifies the state of the military camp.

The *Treatises of Song* <note>original: Song Zhi (宋志); likely the "Treatise on Astronomy" within the *History of Song*.</note> say:
> Solar halos and similar vapors occur when the <term>Vapors of Heaven and Earth <note>The complementary forces of Yin and Yang interacting in the atmosphere.</note></term> interact but are not perfectly sealed. If they do not produce wind and rain, they should be taken as a sign of the army; they are an image of a military camp. Specifically, those with <term>Embracing Ear-rings <note>original: baoer (抱珥); parhelia (sun dogs) that appear to curve or "hug" the sun.</note></term>, cloud-vapors, and <term>Carrying Rainbows <note>original: tihong (提虹); arcs that appear to support or "carry" the weight of the sun or other arcs.</note></term> piercing through them are especially relevant to military affairs.

The *Precious Canon of Heaven and Earth* <note>original: Qiankun Baodian (乾坤寶典); a classical text on divination and cosmology.</note> says:
> A halo that forms a complete circle <note>original: zhouza (周匝); a full 360-degree ring.</note> is an image of military prestige.

<summary>This page details the prophetic meanings of solar halos, distinguishing between black halos that predict floods or political downfall and multi-colored arcs that signal military activity and environmental changes. These omens were crucial for advisors to determine the success of military campaigns and the stability of the imperial court.</summary>

# Divination of the Sun with a Red Halo
# Divination of the Sun with a Blue-Green Halo

<image-desc>A landscape painting depicting a sun surrounded by a thick red halo. Below the sky is a traditional Chinese house with a tiled roof, set among rocky terrain and trees with autumn-colored leaves.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), a preeminent Song Dynasty philosopher whose commentaries on natural phenomena were highly influential.</note> says:
> If the color is red, there will be sweltering rain and thunderclaps.

The *Divinations of the Kaiyuan Era* <note>original: Kaiyuan Zhan (開元占); refers to the *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, a massive 8th-century astrological compendium.</note> say:
> A sun with a <term>Red Halo <note>original: chiyun (赤暈); a reddish atmospheric ring around the sun, often interpreted as a sign of heat or turbulence.</note></term> means there will certainly be heavy rain, lightning, thunderclaps, hail, or extreme heat.

The *Book of Sui* <note>original: Sui Shu (隋書); the official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618 CE), which includes a "Treatise on Celestial Officials" documenting such omens.</note> says:
> If the solar halo is red on the inside and blue-green on the outside, the various ministers will be in harmony with the sovereign.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A landscape painting featuring a sun with a distinct green-blue halo. The scenery below shows a sharp mountain peak and steep, craggy hills populated with pine trees.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:
> If the color is blue-green, then the <term>price of grain <note>original: di (糴); specifically refers to the buying of grain.</note></term> will be high and there will be great winds.

The *Divinations of the Kaiyuan Era* say:
> A sun with a <term>Blue-Green Halo <note>original: qingyun (青暈); the color 'qing' covers the spectrum of blue and green and is traditionally associated with the element of wood and the season of spring.</note></term> means that before ten days have passed, there will be great winds, the price of grain will become expensive, and many people will fall ill.

<summary>This page describes the omens associated with red and blue-green solar halos, correlating their appearance with extreme weather, economic fluctuations, and the health of the populace. While red halos generally signal storms, a specific red-and-green combination is interpreted as a positive sign of political unity.</summary>

# Divination of the Sun with a Yellow Halo

<image-desc>A colored landscape illustration depicting a red sun surrounded by a soft yellow halo in a light grey-blue sky. The *Divinations of the Kaiyuan Era* <note>The *Kaiyuan Zhanjing*, an 8th-century encyclopedia of Chinese astronomy and divination.</note> say:

The *Book of Sui* <note>The official history of the Sui Dynasty, compiled in the 7th century, containing extensive records of omens.</note> says:
> A yellow solar halo indicates that <term>earthworks <note>original: tugong (土功); large-scale construction or corvée labor projects, which often strained the resources of the common people.</note></term> will be mobilized, and the people will be uneasy.

# Divination of a Sun with a Partial Halo

**[Image: A landscape painting inside a rectangular border. In the upper center is a bright red sun. To its lower-left is a partial green crescent-shaped halo. The landscape features rocky, mist-shrouded mountains, a small traditional Chinese building with a blue roof nestled in the hills, and several pine and deciduous trees.]**

Master Zhu Wengong <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher whose views on natural phenomena as "responses" to human governance were standard in later imperial China.</note> says:
> In the direction where the partial halo is located, the army of that quarter will be victorious in battle.

The *Treatise of the Song* <note>Original: *Song Zhi* (宋志). This refers to the astronomical or "Five Elements" records found in the official *History of Song*, which cataloged celestial anomalies as political portents.</note> says:
> If a halo is not complete, the army in the direction where the partial halo is located will be victorious. If a partial halo enters the sun and faces outward toward the four directions, then in the direction it faces, their <term>Ambush Forces<note>Original: 伏 (fú). This refers to hidden troops or clandestine military operations meant to catch an opponent off guard.</note></term> will enter the <term>Central Kingdom<note>Original: 中國 (Zhōngguó). At the time, this referred to the central dynastic state, distinguishing it from the "peripheral" or "barbarian" regions.</note></term>.

The *Universal Divination of Past and Present* <note>Original: *Gu Jin Tong Zhan*. A comprehensive compendium of astrological and meteorological omens.</note> says:
> If a solar halo is incomplete and forms "two embraces" <note>Original: 兩抱 (liǎng bào). This describes two curved segments of a halo flanking the sun like a pair of arms. In traditional divination, such a split or incomplete circle suggested a fractured or contested authority.</note>, it is inauspicious.

# Divination of a Partial Halo like a Net Cover

**[Image: A landscape painting inside a rectangular border. In the upper center is a bright red sun with a green crescent-shaped halo curved over the top like a cap or lid. Below is a scene with a body of water or shore, a small pavilion on a rocky slope, and several trees with sparse foliage.]**

Master Zhu Wengong says:
> If there is a shape like the lid of a <term>Fishing Net<note>Original: 罛 (gū). A specific type of large net; the term describes a halo that arches over the top of the sun like a canopy.</note></term> atop the sun, there are those who desire a <term>Marriage Alliance<note>Original: 和親 (héqīn). A "peace marriage," a strategic diplomatic practice where a member of the imperial family was married to a foreign ruler to secure a border treaty or cessation of hostilities.</note></term>.

The *Treatise of the Song* says:
> A partial halo above the sun shaped like a net cover signifies a desire for a marriage alliance; another interpretation says it signifies <term>Military Action<note>Original: 兵 (bīng). This term literally means "soldiers" or "weapons," but in divination, it serves as a shorthand for the movement of troops or the outbreak of war.</note></term>.

<summary>This page describes the divinatory meanings of partial solar halos, specifically linking their orientation to military victory and the threat of foreign ambushes. It also details a specific "net-shaped" halo that indicates either a diplomatic marriage alliance or impending military conflict.</summary>

## Divination of a Doubled Partial Halo

**[Image: A colored landscape painting within a rectangular border. In the upper right sky, a red sun is depicted with two concentric green arcs (partial haloes) on its right side. Below, a landscape features green rolling hills, trees, and a small dark-roofed pavilion perched on a cliffside.]**

Master Zhu Wengong <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian scholar. His inclusion here lends authority to these astrological interpretations.</note> says:

If a partial halo is doubled, the people of the nation will flourish and multiply.

The *Treatise of the Song* <note>Original: *Song Zhi* (宋志). Specifically, the "Treatise on Astronomy" or the "Treatise on the Five Elements" within the *History of Song*, which recorded celestial omens as reflections of imperial governance.</note> says:

If a partial halo is doubled, the people of the nation will flourish and multiply; it will be a year of <term>Great Harvest<note>Original: 大稔 (dà rěn). A term used in classical texts to denote an exceptionally bountiful year for grain and crops.</note></term>.

## Divination of the Sun with Two Partial Halos

**[Image: A colored landscape painting within a rectangular border. In the sky, a red sun is flanked by two green semi-circular haloes. The landscape below shows a rocky mountain with pine trees and a white building with a dark-tiled roof situated on a slope.]**

Master Zhu Wengong says:

When two halves face each other, there will be great winds throughout the realm.

The *Treatise of the Song* says:

When the sun has two partial halos, great winds shall arise.

The *Book of Sui* <note>Original: *Sui Shu* (隋書). The official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618), which contains extensive records on omens and portents.</note> says:

If a partial halo faces the south, the <term>Northern Tribes<note>Original: 北夷人 (běi yí rén). A historical term for non-Han ethnic groups residing to the north of the Chinese heartland, often viewed in these texts as potential military rivals or invaders.</note></term> intend to revolt and enter the country.

# Divination of a Square Halo Like a Well-Frame

**[Image: A landscape painting with tall, jagged mountain peaks and pine trees. Above the peaks, a red sun is centered within a square-shaped green halo against a pale blue sky.]**

Master Zhu Wengong <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian philosopher of the Song Dynasty. His citations in this manuscript serve to provide intellectual and moral authority to the astrological predictions.</note> says:

> If a square halo appears like a <term>well-frame<note>Original: 井榦 (jǐng gàn). The wooden railing or framework surrounding the mouth of a traditional well, usually square in shape.</note></term>, the world will not be at peace and there will be war.

The *Treatise of the Song* <note>The "Treatise on Astronomy" within the *History of Song* (Song Shi), which recorded celestial events as omens reflecting the emperor's virtue or the state's health.</note> says:

> When a halo is square like a well-frame, the realm will be in discord; one day, great armies shall rise.

The *Book of Sui* <note>The official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618), compiled during the subsequent Tang Dynasty.</note> says:

> When a solar halo is like a well-frame, the state already has great armies.

# Divination of a Solar Halo Like a Well-Wall and Carriage Wheel

**[Image: A landscape painting featuring a traditional Chinese building with a green-tiled roof on the left, nestled against a cliff. On the right are rounded hills and trees. Above, a red sun is enclosed by a square green border, which is itself encircled by a larger round green halo.]**

Master Zhu Wengong says:

> A halo like a <term>well-wall<note>Original: 井垣 (jǐng yuán). Referring to a low wall or enclosure around a well.</note></term> and a carriage wheel indicates two enemy states will use their armies to destroy nations.

The *Treatise of the Song* says:

> If a halo appears like a well-wall and a carriage wheel, two nations shall perish by the sword.

The *Book of Sui* says:

> When a solar halo like a carriage wheel appears to the left or right of the sun, armies will arise and cities will fall.

# Divination of Intersecting Solar Halos

**[Image: An illustration depicting a solar phenomenon known as "intersecting halos." A central sun, shown as a solid red circle, is surrounded by a circular green halo. A second green circular halo of equal size intersects the first one to its right. The landscape below features a high, craggy mountain peak on the right, several vertical, pillar-like rocks in the center, and sparse trees growing on a low hill in the foreground.]**

Master <term>Zhu Wengong<note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), a preeminent Neo-Confucian scholar whose writings on natural philosophy and ethics were authoritative in the later imperial period.</note></term> says:

> When intersecting halos appear like <term>linked rings<note>Original: 連環 (liánhuán). A series of interlocking circles.</note></term> and pierce the sun, armies will rise and struggle against one another.

The *Treatise of Song* <note>The astronomical records found in the official *History of Song*.</note> says:

> Intersecting halos signify that two armies will rise to fight over territory. If they <term>pierce<note>Original: 貫 (guàn). This refers to the arc of a halo appearing to pass directly through the disc of the sun.</note></term> the sun, there will be a defeated army below.

The *Book of Sui* <note>The official history of the Sui Dynasty, which includes extensive records on omens and celestial portents.</note> says:

> If the sun has thick intersecting halos, there are those among the sovereign’s inner circle who are in conflict.

# Divination of a Solar Halo with Two Opposed Arcs Above and Below

**[Image: An illustration of a solar halo with tangent arcs. A solid red sun is centered within a circular green halo. Directly above the halo is an upward-curving green arc, and directly below it is a downward-curving green arc. The landscape below shows a series of rounded green hills with several pine trees. A taller, jagged mountain peak is visible in the background on the right.]**

Master Zhu Wengong says:

> When a square halo gathers two <term>opposed arcs<note>Original: 背 (bèi), literally "backs." In Chinese uranology, these are arcs that curve away from the sun, such as tangent arcs or circumzenithal arcs.</note></term> at the top and bottom, the people will perish and the generals will be defeated.

The *Treatise of Song* says:

> When a square halo has two opposed arcs gathered above and below, the generals will be defeated and the people will perish.

The *Book of Sui* says:

> If there are two opposed arcs above and below a halo: if there is no war, then armies shall rise; if there is already war, the armies will be defeated.

### Divination of a Double Solar Halo

**[Image: A colored illustration of a meteorological phenomenon. A red sun is positioned in the upper left, encircled by two concentric halos—the inner ring is yellow and the outer ring is blue. Beneath the sky is a landscape of sharp, blue-grey mountain peaks and dark clusters of trees.]**

Master <term>Zhu Wengong<note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian scholar of the Song Dynasty. His commentaries on the classics and natural world were considered authoritative for centuries.</note></term> says:

If the halo appears in two layers, the sovereign <note>Original: 人君 (rénjūn), referring to the emperor or ruler.</note> possesses virtue.

The <term>Treatise of Song<note>Referring to the astronomical and omen-related chapters within the *Song Shi* (Official History of the Song Dynasty).</note></term> says:

A double halo means the sovereign possesses virtue. It also says: it signifies the appointment of marquises and kings. Alternatively, it suggests that if a battle is fought in a single day, the enemy cannot be overcome.

<column-break/>

### Divination of Solar Halos Intersecting Like Linked Rings

**[Image: A colored illustration showing a complex solar halo. A red sun is set within two interlocking green rings, similar to a chain link. The landscape below consists of dark, jagged mountains on the left with visible pine trees and a gentler green hill on the right.]**

Master Zhu Wengong says:

When solar halos appear like <term>linked rings<note>Original: 連環 (liánhuán). This describes an atmospheric phenomenon where two circular arcs intersect, resembling links in a chain.</note></term> and pierce through the sun, two armies will struggle against one another.

The *Treatise of Song* says:

Halos appearing like linked rings signify that troops will rise to fight over territory.

Regarding the sun and moon: two enemies face each other; those who follow the <gloss>natural or cosmic order</gloss> will achieve victory.

If the halo <term>pierces<note>Original: 貫 (guàn). In traditional meteorology, this refers to a halo or arc passing directly through the center of the solar or lunar disk, usually interpreted as a sign of violent intrusion or upheaval.</note></term> the sun, an army will be defeated and a new general will rise.

The <term>Book of Sui<note>The official history of the Sui Dynasty (581–618 CE), which contains detailed records of celestial omens and their political interpretations.</note></term> says:

Halos in the form of linked rings mean that two armies of soldiers will rise to fight over territory.

## Divination of a Fourfold Solar Halo

**[Image: An illustration of a red sun centered within four concentric green rings in a pale sky. Below is a landscape with several jagged blue-green mountain peaks of varying heights.]**

Master <term>Zhu Wengong<note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian scholar of the Song Dynasty. His inclusion here lends authority to these meteorological interpretations.</note></term> says:

When the halo appears in four layers, the army will be defeated in the open wilderness, and beneath the heavens, there are <term>rebellious ministers<note>Original: 叛臣 (pànchén), officials who betray the ruler or the state.</note></term>.

The <term>Treatise of Song<note>Referring to the astronomical chapters of the *Song Shi* (Official History of the Song Dynasty), which recorded celestial omens and their historical outcomes.</note></term> says:

If a fourfold solar halo appears and there is an army in the field, it will suffer defeat; if there is no army currently in the field, it signifies that there are rebellious ministers beneath the sun.

# Divination of Solar Halos with Hugging and Earring Arcs

<image-desc>A colored illustration depicting a complex solar phenomenon. The sun is represented by a central red disc surrounded by a thin green halo. To the left, additional multi-colored crescent-shaped symbols of atmospheric phenomena are visible. The landscape below consists of a windswept hill with sparse trees and several distinct, vertical rock pillars standing in the background.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong). Referring to the Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi, who integrated natural observations into his moral and political philosophy.</note> says:

Those specific types that possess "hugging" arcs <note>original: 抱 (bao). These are arcs that appear to curve toward or "embrace" the sun.</note> and "earrings" <note>original: 珥 (er). A technical term for parhelia or "sun dogs"—bright spots that appear on either side of the sun.</note> primarily govern military affairs.

The Treatises of Song <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi). The "Treatise on Celestial Phenomena" from the official history of the Song Dynasty.</note> say:

When the text mentions "types of these phenomena," it refers to more than just the "hugging" category alone.

# Divination of Solar Halos in the Directions of Mao, Chen, and Si

<image-desc>A colored illustration of a solar halo. The sun, a solid red circle, is encircled by a wide, layered halo of blue and yellow-gold. The sky is light blue. Literally the "Son of Heaven."</note> is anxious for the welfare of the people; there will be heavy rain within the month.

# Divination of Hugging and Earring Arcs Outside the Halo

<image-desc>A hand-colored woodblock illustration depicting an atmospheric phenomenon. At the center is a red sun surrounded by a multi-colored halo (green and red rings). Two pairs of reddish-brown curved arcs, identified as "bào ěr" (parhelia or sundogs), are positioned outside the main halo. Below the sky, the landscape consists of stylized rocky cliffs on the right with trees on top, and a lower rocky formation on the left near a body of water.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong). Referring to the influential Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi, whose works often touched upon the relationship between celestial "patterns" and earthly events.</note> says:

When the "hugging" <note>original: 抱 (bao); atmospheric arcs that appear to curve toward or "embrace" the sun.</note> and "earrings" <note>original: 珥 (er); technical term for parhelia or "sun dogs," which are bright spots or short arcs appearing on either side of the sun.</note> are positioned outside the halo, it is advantageous for the "outsiders" <note>the attacking or besieging force</note> who are attacking a city.

The Treatises of Song <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi). The astronomical and meteorological records found in the official History of the Song Dynasty.</note> say:

If there is one hugging arc and one earring arc outside the halo, the outsiders will be victorious.

# Divination of Solar Halos with Hugging and Earring Arcs Inside

<image-desc>A hand-colored woodblock illustration showing solar phenomena. A red sun is enclosed by a green and red halo. The landscape below features tall, craggy mountains in the distance on the left, and a rocky shoreline with green trees on the right.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:

When the hugging and earring arcs are located inside the halo, if a city is being besieged <note>original: 圖城 (tu cheng); literally "to plot against" or "map out" a city, referring to military strategy or a siege.</note>, then those inside the city will be victorious.

The Treatises of Song say:

If there are hugging and earring arcs inside the halo, during a siege, the people within the army <note>referring to the defending garrison</note> inside the city will be victorious.

# Divination of a Solar Halo with One Embracing and One Opposing Arc

<image-desc>A colored illustration of a mountain landscape with trees. In the sky, a central red sun is enclosed in a multi-layered circular halo (yellow and blue). Flanking the central sun are two crescent-shaped arcs: the arc on the right curves toward the sun ("embrace"), while the arc on the left curves away from it ("back").</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong). Referring to the renowned philosopher Zhu Xi (1130–1200), whose authority was often cited in matters of natural philosophy.</note> says:

A halo accompanied by an embracing arc and an opposing arc signifies defeat for one's own side.

The Treatises of Song <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi). The "Treatise on Astronomy" within the official History of the Song Dynasty.</note> say:

When a halo has one embracing arc and one opposing arc, it means the army will be destroyed and one's own side will be defeated; it also signifies internal discord.

The Book of Jin <note>original: 晉書 (Jin Shu). The official history of the Jin Dynasty, compiled in the 7th century, which contains extensive records on celestial omens.</note> says:

The presence of one embracing arc and one opposing arc beside the sun signifies a breakthrough. The "embracing" arc <term>bào; 抱 <gloss>an arc curving toward the sun</gloss></term> represents favorable energy <note>original: 順氣 (shunqi); energy that flows in harmony with the natural or intended order.</note>, while the "opposing" arc <term>bèi; 背 <gloss>an arc curving away from the sun</gloss></term> represents contrary energy <note>original: 逆氣 (niqi); rebellious or oppositional energy.</note>. When two armies face each other, the side aligned with the favorable embracing arc that attacks the side with the contrary opposing arc will be victorious, causing the enemy to break and flee.

<column-break/>

# Divination of a Solar Halo with a Straight Earring Arc

<image-desc>A colored illustration of a landscape featuring rocks, a small bridge, and pine trees. In the sky, a red sun is surrounded by concentric green and blue rings. A straight, horizontal red line (珥, "ear" or arc) pierces through the center of the sun and its halos.</image-desc>

Master Zhu says:

A halo with a straight earring arc <term>ěr; 珥 <gloss>literally "earring"; a technical term for a parhelion or sun dog appearing at the side of the sun</gloss></term> signifies the destruction of the army.

The Treatises of Song say:

A halo with a straight earring arc means the army will be destroyed. If the arc pierces through the sun, it signifies slaughter.

# Divination of a Solar Halo with Two Ears Pierced by Thick Clouds

<image-desc>A colored illustration of an atmospheric solar phenomenon. A central red sun is enclosed by a circular halo with green and red rings. Two horizontal red lines, described as "ears" (珥), extend from the sides of the halo. Four vertical, multi-colored strokes intersect these "ears." Below the celestial display is a landscape in ink and light color, featuring a small pavilion with a tiered roof on a shoreline, surrounded by pine trees and a jagged cliff on the right.</image-desc>

Master Zhu <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong). Referring to the renowned Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi (1130–1200), whose commentaries on natural phenomena were highly influential.</note> says:

When a halo has two ears <term>ěr; 珥 <gloss>parhelia or "sun dogs," which appear as bright spots or tufts of light on the sides of a solar halo</gloss></term> and thick clouds pierce through them, the year will be filled with much illness and disease.

The Treatises of Song <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi). Refers to the "Treatise on Astronomy" within the official History of the Song Dynasty.</note> say:

A halo with two ears pierced by clouds signifies that sickness will prevail.

# Divination of a Solar Halo with "Four Backs" within the Interior

# Divination of a Solar Halo with Embraces, "Ears," Backing Vapors, and a Piercing White Rainbow

# Divination of a Solar Halo with One Crown, One Knot, and One Ear

# Divination of a Solar Halo with Four Ears, Four Backings, and Four Slit-Rings

<image-desc>A rectangular illustration depicting a complex solar halo system. # Divination of a Solar Halo with "Ears"

# Divination of Solar Halos with "Embracing Vapors" and "White Rainbows Piercing the Sun"

<image-desc>A landscape painting with jagged, ink-wash mountain peaks. In the sky above, a red sun is surrounded by a golden circular halo. To the right of the sun, a pale white crescent-shaped arc, described as "embracing" (抱), appears.</image-desc>

**The Treatise of the History of Song** <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi). The "Treatise on Astronomy" within the official dynastic history of the Song.</note> states:

A halo with a single "embrace" is considered a favorable sign. If an arc pierces the halo: if it is to the west of the sun, the army to the west will be victorious; if it is to the east of the sun, the eastern army will win. The same logic applies to all four cardinal directions.

<image-desc>A landscape painting depicting green and blue-toned mountains. In the sky, a red sun is encircled by a golden halo. To its left is a prominent red crescent-shaped arc, representing a "parhelion" or "ear" (珥).</image-desc>

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

A halo with ears indicates sudden conflict within the palace. If this occurs in the spring, the **Heir Apparent** will be replaced. Others say it means a minister is plotting. If an army is currently abroad, that outside army will meet with misfortune.

# Divination of a Solar Eclipse with Strong Winds

<image-desc>A landscape illustration depicting a solar eclipse under a dark, stormy sky. The sun is represented by two overlapping circles, one red and one black. Dark grey clouds fill the sky above a landscape of stylized mountains and vegetation.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong); refers to the Neo-Confucian philosopher Zhu Xi.</note> says:

If there is a solar eclipse accompanied by strong winds, it signifies that the **Chancellor** <term>original: 宰相 (zaixiang); the highest-ranking government official, often serving as the primary advisor to the Emperor</term> is monopolizing power.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi); the "Treatise on Astronomy" within the official dynastic history of the Song period.</note> states:

When a solar eclipse occurs with strong winds and clouds appearing in all four directions, it indicates that the **Chancellor** is usurping authority and intends to rebel.

<column-break/>

# Divination of a Solar Halo with a Single "Back Aura"

<image-desc>A mountainous landscape with pine trees. In the sky, a red sun is surrounded by a multi-colored circular halo of blue, red, and yellow. To the left of the halo, there is a red crescent-shaped atmospheric phenomenon called a 'back aura' (bei qi).</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** says:

If a halo has a **back aura** <term>original: 背 (bei); an atmospheric arc that curves away from the sun, appearing to "turn its back" on it</term>, there will certainly be rebellious bandits in the region where it points.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

A halo with a single "back aura" indicates the presence of rebellious ministers. If the arc is in the East, there are rebels in the East; if the army rebels there, the same logic applies to the other three cardinal directions. It is also said:

When a halo and a "back aura" appear together, war will arise, and the affected region will lose its cities.

<image-desc>A color illustration of a solar eclipse occurring over a mountainous landscape. A black disk is shown partially covering a red sun. **The Treatise of the History of Song** <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi); specifically the "Treatise on Astronomy" within the official history of the Song Dynasty.</note> states:

If during a solar eclipse there is an **ominous vapor** <term>original: 妖氣 (yaoqi); literally "strange" or "demon" vapor, indicating a supernatural warning</term> like a rainbow above the sun, it signifies that ministers close to the Emperor are rebelling against their sovereign. # Divination of a Solar Eclipse with Earthquakes and Extreme Cold

<image-desc>A color illustration of a solar eclipse. A black disk overlaps a red sun in the upper right. The landscape below features a high, craggy cliff with trees on the left and a smaller hill with several pine trees on the right.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** says:

If an eclipse occurs and is accompanied by extreme cold, then **foreign invaders** <term>original: 夷狄 (Yidi); a collective term used historically to refer to non-Chinese tribes or "barbarians" to the North and West</term> will arrive.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

When a solar eclipse occurs alongside an earthquake, and the sun appears **dim and lusterless** <note>original: 色味 (sewei); literally "color and flavor," here referring to the sun's physical appearance and vitality</note> while the weather turns cold, it indicates that the high nobility are monopolizing power. If there is extreme cold, the **foreign invaders** will mobilize their armies for war.

### Divination of the Moon Being Large and Bright

<image-desc>A colored landscape illustration showing a large, bright full moon in the sky. Inside the moon is the silhouette of a rabbit (the Jade Rabbit). The moon illuminates a night scene of a rocky hillside with sparse trees.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong); referring to the scholar Zhu Xi.</note> says:

The moon signifies "to wane" <note>original: 闕 (que); the character implies a gap or deficiency, referring to the moon's cyclical nature</note>; it is the master of the **Yin principle** and represents the **ministers**.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

The moon is the essence of **Great Yin** <term>Great Yin: Taiyin (太陰), the cosmic force associated with the feminine, the moon, and the receptive</term>. "Waning" refers to the law that once fullness reaches its extreme, it must necessarily diminish. Its essence governs the night; it manifests as Yin, the Empress, the ministers, wives and concubines, and the element of **Water**.

**The Commentary on the Book of Changes by Jing Fang** <note>Jing Fang (77–37 BCE) was a Han dynasty scholar famous for his expertise in the I Ching and atmospheric divination.</note> says:

When the realm is at peace and both those of high and low status prosper together, then the moon appears **large and bright**.

### Divination of a Solar Eclipse with Two or Four "Ears"

<image-desc>A colored landscape illustration depicting solar phenomena. In the sky, a solar eclipse is shown as a dark disc partially obscuring a red one. Flanking this are several pairs of colored arcs, representing "ears" (solar halos or parhelia). The phenomena are set above a green and gray mountainous landscape with trees.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** says:

If during a solar eclipse there are **two "ears"** or **four "ears"** <term>original: 珥 (er); these are solar halos or "sun dogs" (parhelia) that appear as luminous arcs or spots on either side of the sun</term> and white clouds emerge from within them, use the sun’s omens to divine the matter.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

If a solar eclipse occurs with **two or four "ears"** and white clouds emerge from within:
*   On a **Jiazi** day <note>The 1st day of the 60-day cycle</note>, there will be war across the realm.
*   On a **Bingzi** day <note>The 13th day of the cycle</note>, there will be pestilence across the realm.
*   On **Wuji** days <note>Days in the cycle associated with the Earth element</note>, there will be war and mourning.
*   On a **Gengshen** day <note>The 57th day of the cycle</note>, those below will pressure those above.
*   On **Rengui** days <note>Days associated with the Water element</note>, great earthworks and construction projects will be initiated.

### Divination of the Moon Appearing in the West on the Last Day of the Month

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese landscape painting shows a thin white crescent moon in a dark sky. Below, stylized mountains with blue and green washes are interspersed with pine trees. A prominent, rounded peak stands in the center-right of the composition.</image-desc>

---

**Master Zhu** <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong); referring to the influential Neo-Confucian scholar Zhu Xi.</note> says:

If the moon appears in the direction of **Dui** <term>Dui: 兌; one of the eight trigrams of the I Ching, corresponding to the West and the element of Metal</term> on the last day of the lunar month <note>original: 晦 (hui); the 30th or final day of the lunar month when the moon is typically dark</note>, it signifies that the ministers and subordinates are arrogant and overbearing.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

When the moon is seen in the West on the last day of the month, it is positioned ahead of the sun. This indicates it is moving too fast. This represents a state of "deficiency" <term>Deficiency: 朒 (nü); a technical term in ancient astronomy for a celestial body moving slower than its calculated speed, or being "behind" its proper station</term> in the sun. It is an omen of a ruler who is too relaxed and indulgent, while his ministers are arrogant, overbearing, and usurping power.

**The Commentary on the Book of Changes by Jing Fang** <note>Jing Fang (77–37 BCE) was a Han dynasty expert in hexagrams and atmospheric divination.</note> says:

When the moon appears in the West on the last day of the month, it is called **Tiao** <term>Tiao: 朓; the phenomenon of the moon appearing in the west on the last day of the month, signifying it is "fast" or "early"</term>. This indicates that the feudal lords and kings are lax and slow in their duties.

**Liu Xiang** <note>A famous Han dynasty scholar and astronomer (77–6 BCE).</note> says:

The term *Tiao* refers to speed. If the ruler is lax, the ministers become arrogant. Because the sun's movement is slow and the moon's movement is fast, it signifies that the lords are willful and the subordinates are aggressive and encroaching; hence, the moon travels with excessive speed.

<column-break/>

### Divination of the Moon Appearing in the East on the First Day of the Month

<image-desc>A traditional Chinese landscape painting features a full moon glowing with a yellow halo, containing the distinct silhouette of a rabbit (the Jade Rabbit). The landscape features a tall, narrow green mountain peak and rocky outcroppings with pine trees under a light sky.</image-desc>

---

**Master Zhu** says:

If the moon appears in the East on the first day of the lunar month <note>original: 朔 (shuo); the first day of the new moon</note>, the ruler must be stern and solemn.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

If the moon is seen in the East on the first day, it is positioned behind the sun. This indicates it is moving too slowly. This is an omen of a "deficiency" in the sun, where the ruler is stern and the ministers are fearful and trembling.

**The Commentary on the Book of Changes by Jing Fang** says:

When the moon appears in the East on the first day, it is called **Fan** <term>Fan: 反; literally "reversal," referring to the moon appearing in the East on the first day of the month when it should be invisible or in the West</term>. *Fan* indicates that the lords and kings are being stern and severe.

**Liu Xiang** considers *Fan* to carry the meaning of "not advancing." When a ruler is stern and demanding, his ministers are filled with dread; therefore, the sun moves quickly while the moon moves slowly, as if the moon does not dare to approach the ruler. When lords and kings withdraw or are unable to fulfill their duties <note>original: 縮朒 (suo nü); to shrink or be deficient</note>, the moon moves slowly.

<summary>This page describes the astrological implications of the moon appearing "out of schedule" on the first and last days of the lunar month. Such anomalies were interpreted as reflections of the political relationship between a ruler (symbolized by the sun) and his ministers (symbolized by the moon).</summary>

<keywords>lunar divination, Zhu Xi, Jing Fang, Liu Xiang, Tiao (early moon), Fan (late moon), ministerial relations, solar and lunar speed, History of Song</keywords>

## Divination on the Moon's Irregular Advancement and Retreat

<image-desc>A colored landscape painting within a rectangular frame. On the upper left, a bright white moon hangs in a pale blue sky. The landscape below features stylized rocky mountains in shades of green and brown, with sparse pine trees. On the far right, a small white building with a dark tiled roof and red accents is nestled at the foot of a tall, pointed mountain peak.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong); the posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian scholar of the Song Dynasty.</note> says:

The "advancement and retreat" of the moon refers to its irregular speed. When it is inconsistent, it signifies that ministers or the Empress are monopolizing political power.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi); specifically the "Treatise on Astronomy" within the official dynastic history of the Song.</note> states:

When ministers, empresses, or imperial relatives <term>Imperial relatives: 外戚 (waiqi); specifically the families of the emperor’s consorts or mother, who often wielded significant political influence</term> monopolize power, the moon will frequently deviate from its proper course. Its movement becomes slow or fast, advancing or retreating irregularly; thus it is said that the moon "undergoes a mutation." To resolve this omen, the sovereign should grant general amnesties, lighten criminal punishments, and show compassion to those in prison <note>original: 恤獄 (xuyu); a traditional practice where the Emperor reviewed court cases to ensure no one was being held unjustly, which was believed to restore cosmic harmony.</note>.

## Divination on the Moon Traveling the Nine Paths relative to the Central Path

<image-desc>A colored landscape painting within a rectangular frame. On the left side, a tall, craggy cliff with pine trees dominates the foreground. In the center, there are lower, rounded green hills. On the upper right, a bright white moon is positioned against a pale blue sky.</image-desc>

**Master Zhu** says:

When the moon travels along the **Yin path** <term>Yin path: 陰道 (yindao); in this context, the northern or interior portion of the lunar orbit</term>, there will be cloudy skies and rain. When it travels along the **Yang path** <term>Yang path: 陽道 (yangdao); the southern or exterior portion of the orbit</term>, there will be drought and wind.

**The Treatise of the History of Song** states:

When an enlightened king is on the throne, the moon’s movement follows the **Nine Paths** <term>Nine Paths: 月行九道 (yuexing jiudao); an ancient astronomical theory describing the lunar orbit—consisting of the ecliptic (Yellow Path) and eight lunar paths (two blue, two red, two white, and two black) that shift over time.</term> correctly, and the moon appears bright and clear on both its upper and lower surfaces.

It suggests that such celestial "mutations" can be corrected through the Emperor's acts of judicial mercy.</summary>

# Divination on the Moon Traveling the Middle Path

**Master Zhu** <note>original: 朱文公 (Zhu Wengong); the posthumous title of Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian philosopher whose interpretations became the standard for the imperial examinations.</note> says:

When the moon travels along the Middle Path, all under heaven is peaceful and serene.

**The Jingyou Divination** <note>original: 景佑占 (Jingyou Zhan); an astrological text compiled during the Jingyou era (1034–1038) of the Northern Song Dynasty.</note> states:

The three gates of heaven are like the four indicators of the "Room" <note>The "Room" (Fang) is one of the 28 Lunar Mansions in ancient Chinese astronomy, located in the constellation Scorpius.</note>. The center is called the Celestial Street; this is the Middle Path of heaven and the Celestial Gate. When the moon follows its proper orbit through the Celestial Street, the world is harmonious and at peace.

**The Yellow River Chart: The Emperor’s Joyful Gaze** <note>original: 河圖帝覽嬉 (Hetu Di Lan Xi); a divinatory text belonging to the "apocryphal" (chenwei) tradition which interpreted celestial signs as political omens.</note> states:

The moon traveling the Middle Path is called "Tranquility," signifying that the world is at peace.

**Jing Fang** <note>A famous scholar of the Han Dynasty (77–37 BCE) known for his expertise in the I Ching and his system of correlating musical pitches with lunar cycles and disasters.</note> says:

Great peace under heaven, an abundant harvest of the five grains, and increased longevity for the sovereign occur when the moon travels through the Gate of the Son of Heaven <note>original: 天子門 (Tianzi men); a symbolic name for the auspicious path of the moon between certain stars.</note>.

Regarding "Yellow Rays": The ruler has prosperity and the empress or consorts have joy when these appear above the moon.

**The Jingzhou Divination** states:

If the moon "wears an aura" <term>Wearing an aura: 戴氣 (daiqi); an atmospheric phenomenon, likely a lunar halo or a parselene (moondog), where a crown-like arc of light appears above the moon's disk.</term>, within one hundred days the sovereign will have cause for joy.

# Divination on the Moon Turning Black and Bright | Divination on the Moon Turning White and Bright

<image-desc>A landscape painting in the upper panel of the left page depicts a dark, brownish-red moon in a greyish sky. Below, a river flows past a hilly bank with trees. A small boat with a thatched roof is moored at the water's edge.</image-desc>

> Black signifies the **Element of Water** and signifies sickness.

**The Treatise of the Song Dynasty** <note>original: 宋志 (Song Zhi); referring to the astronomical and ominal records in the official History of the Song.</note> states:
> Black signifies the Element of Water and signifies sickness.

**The Chart of Talismans and Omens** <note>original: 符瑞圖 (Furui Tu); a text documenting signs that prove a ruler possesses the "Mandate of Heaven."</note> states:

# Divination on the Moon being Deficient on the West before the Full Moon and Deficient on the East after the Full Moon

<image-desc>A landscape illustration depicting mountains and stylized trees under a sky containing two lunar figures.
