The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: *Sòng Zhì* (宋志); likely referring to the "Book of Song" (Song Shu), specifically the chapters on "Five Phases" or "Astronomy" which record omens and their meanings.</note> states: On a **Jia** day <note>The first of the ten Heavenly Stems, associated with the element of Wood and the beginning of cycles.</note>, a great wind indicates that war will arise at sea.

The *Treasury of Heaven and Earth* <note>original: *Qiánkūn Bǎodiǎn* (乾坤寶典); a classical reference work on cosmology and divination.</note> states: If there is a great wind on a **Jia** day, it must be followed by rain on the **Bing** or **Ding** days. If it does not rain, then war will arise at sea.

On an **Yi** day, foreign tribes will come to invade.

The *Treatise of Song* states: A great wind on an **Yi** day causes the price of grain <note>original: *sù* (粟); specifically millet, the staple food of northern China.</note> to become expensive and foreign tribes to invade the borders.

On **Bing** or **Ding** days <note>Stems associated with the element of Fire.</note>, there will be drought and pestilence, and border troops will besiege cities.

The *Treatise of Song* states: A great wind on a **Bing** day means border troops are planning urgent maneuvers; a great wind on a **Ding** day indicates drought and pestilence.

On **Wu** or **Ji** days <note>Stems associated with the element of Earth.</note>, the price of purchased grain rises and laborers for earthworks <term>earthworks: *tǔgōng* (土工); large-scale construction projects involving soil, such as building city walls or dikes.</term> will be relocated.

The *Treatise of Song* states: Great winds on **Wu** or **Ji** days mean that both earthwork labor and food prices will become expensive, or people will be forced to relocate their towns.

On **Geng** or **Xin** days <note>Stems associated with the element of Metal.</note>, if the wind "cries out in anger" <note>Referring to high-pitched or howling wind sounds.</note>, one must urgently repair the borders and strengthen defenses; then there will be no blame.

The *Treatise of Song* states: On **Geng** or **Xin** days, if the sound of the wind is like shouting and anger, it is appropriate to repair the borders.

<column-break/>

On **Ren** or **Gui** days <note>Stems associated with the element of Water.</note>, flying sand indicates that northern enemies will invade the territory and cause unrest.

The *Treatise of Song* states: On **Ren** or **Gui** days, if the wind blows sand and snaps trees, northern enemies will invade the borders.

If it rains within three days of the above events, then the "anger of **Yang**" is resolved. It is beneficial to receive it with **Yin** <note>In this context, the wind is an active, aggressive "Yang" force. Rain, being "Yin," acts as a soothing or neutralizing counter-balance.</note>.

Jing Fang <note>A Han dynasty scholar famous for his work on the I Ching and atmospheric divination.</note> states: Wind is **Yang** and rain is **Yin**. When Yang is in a state of anger but encounters Yin, the tension is therefore resolved.

A **Zi** day <note>The first of the twelve Earthly Branches, associated with the Rat and the direction North.</note> indicates war arising from within the waters.

The *Treatise of Song* states: On a **Zi** day, a great wind and dim sunlight mean war will arise from within the waters.

A **Chou** day <note>The second Earthly Branch, associated with the Ox and late winter.</note> is a sign that grain will become expensive.

The *Treatise of Song* states: On a **Chou** day, a great wind that sweeps the ground and raises sand means grain prices will suddenly skyrocket.

A **Yin** day <note>The third Earthly Branch, associated with the Tiger and early spring.</note> indicates there is "red vapor" in the sky, signaling disaster.

The *Treatise of Song* states: On a **Yin** day, a great wind and red vapor filling the four directions mean there will be a fire disaster.

### Observing Victory or Defeat in War through Wind Divination

<summary>This page details the prognostications for the final nine Earthly Branches, linking specific wind conditions to social and natural events like locust swarms, droughts, and military invasions. It concludes by citing the authority of the scholar Jing Fang and introducing a section on military divination.</summary>

--- Page 306 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of wind-based prognostications, moving from the specific Earthly Branch days (Mao, Chen, Si, Wu, Wei) onto general military tactics and the "Nayin" system of musical-elemental correspondences used to predict victory or defeat in battle.</meta>

If the wind comes from the **Zi** or **Wu** palaces <note>North and South directions respectively.</note>, the host <note>The "Host" (*zhǔ*) usually refers to the defending party or the local commander, while the "Guest" (*kè*) refers to the invader or the newcomer.</note> will suffer a great defeat. This wind also signifies success in besieging a city or that a border town will be captured; other directions should be interpreted following this logic. If wind and rain clash during the movement of troops, the army will suffer a total defeat, and their names will perish along with their corpses.

> The *Treatise of Song* <note>original: *Sòng Zhì* (宋志)</note> states: When an army first sets out and during the first three days of the march, if the wind is vigorous and blows against the troops, making the banners difficult to lift, the voices of the men sounding fearful, and the horses constantly restless; if it blows sand and drives dust so that the footprints of passing men and horses are instantly erased, this is called a **Ghost Wind** <note>original: *guǐfēng* (鬼風)</note>. If, within three days of setting out or during a battle, there is a sudden wind and the rain soaks the men and horses so that they cannot rally, this indicates the army will be defeated. If the sky is dark, the sound of the wind is chaotic, or if there is prolonged overcast weather without rain, these are all signs of conspiracies being hatched by subordinates; one should devise counter-strategies to better align with the will of Heaven. It also says: If a whirlwind suddenly arrives as the army sets out, snapping the main banner <term>main banner: *yáqí* (牙旗); the ceremonial flag representing the commander's authority.</term>, or if the flags wrap around their poles or hang down listlessly, the general will die in battle. If the camp formations are already established and a sudden storm covers the area, toppling the army tents and breaking flags and trees, it is an evil omen of desertion, where the commanding general loses his troops to rebellion and scattering. The *Divination of Wind Perception* <note>original: *Fēngjué Zhàn* (風覺占)</note> states: If there is no wind and the plants do not move when the army first sets out, the enemy cannot be captured. If the flags point forward during the march, the three armies will suffer a great defeat and the general will die. If enemies are encountered mid-way...

<column-break/>

...when two armies cross paths, use wind divination to determine victory or defeat. First, clarify the **Nayin** <term>Nayin: *nàyīn* (納音); 'Melodic Elements,' a system that correlates the sixty-year cycle with musical tones and the Five Elements to determine cosmic resonance.</term> of that day. Next, divine the time and direction of the wind's origin. The *Nayin* of the day represents the **Guest**, while the time and the direction from which the wind comes represent the **Host**.

> The *Treatise of Song* states: When two armies face one another and the outcome is not yet clear, take the time of divination and the direction of the wind as the **Host**, and the *Nayin* of the day as the **Guest**. If the time and direction "overcome" <note>Referring to the Five Elements theory (Wu Xing) where one element conquers another.</note> the *Nayin* tone, it is favorable for the Host to wait and respond to the enemy. If the *Nayin* overcomes the time and direction, it is favorable for the Guest to strike first. If the elements "generate" <note>Mutually support</note> one another, it signifies harmony and a lack of conflict.

> The *Treatise of Song* states: If the time and the direction from which the wind comes can overcome the *Nayin*, the Host wins; otherwise, the Guest wins. If they are in a state of mutual generation, they are in "comparison and harmony" <note>original: *bǐhé* (比和)</note>, and there will be no battle.
**Zi** and **Wu** correspond to the **Gong** note <note>The first note of the pentatonic scale, associated with Earth and the Emperor.</note>.

**Mao** and **You** correspond to the **Yu** note <note>The fifth note, associated with Water and darkness.</note>.
**Chen** and **Xu** correspond to the **Shang** note <note>The second note, associated with Metal and justice or destruction.</note>.
**Si** and **Hai** correspond to the **Jue** note <note>The third note, associated with Wood and growth.</note>.

> The *Precious Canon of Heaven and Earth* <note>original: *Qiánkūn Bǎodiǎn* (乾坤寶典)</note> states: For example, the days of **Ren-zi**, **Gui-chou**, **Ren-wu**, **Gui-wei**, **Wu-chen**, and **Ji-si** are all Wood days <note>In the Nayin system, these pairs are associated with the Wood element.</note>. If the day is the Guest, and the wind comes from the **Chen** or **Xu** directions (the **Shang** note), and the time of the event also falls under **Chen** or **Xu**, the Host will win and the Guest army will be defeated. <meta>This page continues the discussion of wind-based prognostications for military movements. When the sky is dark and murky, the wind is biting and fierce, and the dust swirls violently, the situation is unfavorable. If, upon entering enemy territory or passing through strategic mountain passes and fortified cities, there occurs wind, rain, thunder, or lightning within three days that follows from behind our army, this is known as **the Dragon and the Tiger providing mutual aid.** In such a case, one must strike quickly, and a great victory is certain.

In times of peace, the meeting of wind and clouds signifies that rain is coming; however, when employing troops, this same "mutual aid of Dragon and Tiger" signifies that one should engage in battle immediately. In these omens, the wind is considered the **Host** <note>The "Host" (*zhǔ*) represents the local or defending commander—in this context, usually the reader's own army.</note> and the clouds are the **Guest** <note>The "Guest" (*kè*) represents the approaching or invading force.</note>. If the wind is tight and strong while the cloud vapor is thin and sparse, the Host will be victorious. If the color of the clouds is thick and they arrive with haste, while the wind is weak and lacks the power to "roar in anger," the Guest will be victorious.

> **The Divination of Wind Angles** <note>original: *Fēngjiǎo Zhàn* (風角占)</note> states: Suppose on a **Jue** <note>The third of the Five Tones, associated with Spring and Wood.</note> day, wind and clouds arrive from the directions of **Chen** and **You** <note>East-Southeast and West respectively.</note>; this is called **The Mother caring for the Child.** If the wind comes from the directions of **Chou, Wei, Yin, or Shen**, this is **The Child supporting the Mother.** In both cases, the army setting out will be victorious and achieve great success.

> **The Secret Strategies of Divine Martiality** <note>original: *Shénwǔ Mìlüè* (神武秘畧)</note> states: The wind is the Dragon and represents the Host; the clouds are the Tiger and represent the Guest.

When the wind comes from the directions associated with the **Gong, Yu, or Shang** tones <note>Three of the Five Tones used in ancient Chinese musicology and correlative cosmology.</note> during the seasons or hours of **Shen, Zi, Hai, or Mao**, it corresponds to the "Punishment and Killing" cycles of the **Zi** and **Wu** positions. If the wind is rapid, cold, and turbid, it indicates that **Qiang** <term>Qiang: *Qiāng* (羗); a historical nomadic people often in conflict with central Chinese dynasties.</term> soldiers are violating the borders, appearing and disappearing suddenly.

<column-break/>

If rain faces the army and the battle fluctuates between starting and stopping, or if the wind blows against the troops so that the banners fly backward and cannot advance, it portends a great defeat. It is also said: if wind and rain come against the army but do not soak their clothes, this is called **Heaven Weeping**; the commander will suffer a total defeat. If wind and rain arrive simultaneously during the heat of battle, this is called a **Corpse-Falling Battle**, and a great defeat is inevitable.

> **The Secret Strategies of Divine Martiality** says: If a wild gale blows dust and soil high into the air, it is unfavorable for the army. One should soothe the troops and perform sacrifices to Heaven and Earth for good fortune. It also says: if a whirlwind enters the camp, it is a sign of great misfortune.

When wind and rain are at one's back during an engagement, the army will achieve a great victory, having received "divine aid."

> **The Treatise of Song** <note>original: *Sòng Zhì* (宋志)</note> states: On the first day the army sets out, if the wind follows from behind, the men will be vigorous and brave, the horses will neigh with spirit, and the banners will be lifted high, pointing toward the enemy's position. If the drums and horns sound clear and resonant, it indicates a total victory. If the wind comes from the South and blows forward, it signifies the help of both Heaven and men; our side will capture the enemy’s grain stores, and the enemy will come to surrender. If the wind rises from the ground and the **Five Tones** <term>Five Tones: *Wǔyīn* (五音); the ancient Chinese pentatonic scale (Gong, Shang, Jue, Zhi, Yu) used here to calculate elemental harmony.</term> are in a "mutually generating" relationship—where the wind's direction "generates" our army's element—it is "the Mother caring for the Child" or "the Child supporting the Mother." If the sky is clear and bright, the men and horses are swift, all ranks are filled with joy, and the wind is smooth and pleasant, the army will be victorious.

### Upon Entering an Enemy City, Attack Speedily

If a whirlwind enters an enemy city, one should follow the path where the wind entered and attack it immediately.
When wind enters palaces, residences, or rooms, one must first reflect upon the **Five Tones** <note>original: *wuyin* (五音); the traditional Chinese pentatonic scale used here to categorize the spiritual frequency of the wind</note>, the **Six Emotions**, and the positions of **Punishment and Virtue** <note>original: *xing-de* (刑德); a dualistic system in ancient Chinese cosmobiology where 'Virtue' represents the creative, life-giving force and 'Punishment' represents the destructive, death-dealing force</note>.
The **Treatise of Song** <note>original: *Song Zhi* (宋志); likely referring to the astronomical treatises in the dynastic history of the Song</note> says: When a whirlwind enters, one should divine its meaning using the Five Tones and Six Emotions. Use the states of **Prosperity, Assistance, Rest, and Entrapment** <note>original: *wang xiang xiu qiu* (旺相休囚); the seasonal strength or weakness of the Five Elements</note> and the directions of Punishment and Virtue to distinguish between sorrow and joy.
If the wind comes from a **Virtue position**, it signifies a lucky event; if it comes from a **Punishment position**, it signifies a cause for concern.

### Virtue Signifies Joy and Celebration

If the wind comes from the **Virtue direction** <note>The direction associated with the 'De' or life-giving influence for that specific year, month, or day.</note> of the year, month, or day, it indicates a joyful, celebratory, and auspicious event.

### Punishment Signifies Sorrow and Trouble

If the wind comes from the **Punishment direction** <note>The direction associated with 'Xing' or the destructive influence for that specific period.</note> of the year, month, or day, it indicates distressing, troublesome, and unlucky events.
If the wind enters a room and scatters clothing or startles people regarding their wealth and goods, even if nothing is actually stolen, it is a cause for great worry.

The commentary states: If, upon deploying the army, a **whirlwind** <note>original: *piaofeng* (瓢風); literally 'gourd wind,' referring to a sudden, swirling gust</note> arrives suddenly, and the **main command banner** <note>original: *yaqi* (牙旗); the 'Ivory Flag' which stood at the commander's tent and represented his authority</note> is snapped or broken, or if the banners wrap themselves around the poles or hang limp, the general will die in battle.
If the wind is sudden and violent, causing the military tents to collapse, both the general and the soldiers will suffer.
The commentary states: If the camp is already established and a violent wind comes to harass the site, toppling the military tents, breaking the banners, or snapping trees, it is an evil omen; the commanding general will lose his position and the soldiers will rebel and scatter.
If a violent wind rises suddenly from the directions of **Punishment or the Grave** <note>original: *xing mu* (刑墓); specific baleful directions in the layout of the Eight Trigrams and the Ten Stems</note>, one must guard against sudden raids and ambushes.
The commentary states: If a swift wind comes from the Punishment direction of the year, month, or day, a sudden enemy is arriving, or there are hidden ambushes ahead or behind to catch the men off guard; one must guard against this with the utmost caution.

## Wind and Rain during Military Campaigns

When the army sets out, if there is wind and rain, it signifies that the commander will defeat the enemy and achieve a great victory. This is known as "Obtaining the Way of Heaven." If the wind follows the army <note>meaning a tailwind</note>, it is auspicious regardless of whether it clashes with the directional alignments. If there is wind but no rain:

> When weapons are readied for the forward march,
> If wind arises without rain, one may proceed.
> You shall surely capture the enemy's cities and lands;
> Seize this moment to win merit and fame.

When an army is on the march or stationed in camp, if the wind blows but the **banners and pennants** <term>jingfan (旌籓); ceremonial and tactical flags used for signaling and unit identification</term> do not move—appearing as if there were no wind at all—this is an auspicious sign that the two opposing armies will not fight.

> If the wind blows but the banners do not flutter,
> Both armies shall reconcile and leave the battlefield.
> There is no need for external envoys to negotiate;
> The banners will naturally turn back toward home.

When wind and rain intersect, a battle will certainly take place. One must carefully observe the speed and urgency of the wind and clouds; following their momentum leads to great victory. When wind and clouds intersect:

<column-break/>

If a whirlwind enters a room and sends clothing flying, one should worry about the theft of property, fires, or burglars.

In general, while marching, if a whirlwind comes to clash with you <note>approaches from the front or intersects the path</note>, it is best to avoid it, stop temporarily, and do not advance.

When traveling on a road, if you encounter a whirlwind clashing with you, you should avoid it and wait for the area to clear before you move forward.

Alas! Auspicious changes and transformations are infinite, and divination records are often scattered and mixed. Therefore, I have extracted the essentials to create this volume of collected annotations, highlighting the main principles through verses of varying lengths. In the winter of the **Renwu year** <note>A year in the 60-year sexagenary cycle, likely 1762, 1822, or 1882 depending on the manuscript's era</note>, with the intent to provide techniques for rectifying the state and assisting the sovereign, one should study this book, consult these diagrams, and recite these verses.

->End of the Rhapsody on Annotated Celestial Diagrams and Strange Phenomena<-

### Rain and Clear Skies Between Two Armies

The song says:

> If it rains on the enemy but is clear for us,
> Heaven weeps for them while we are favored.
> But if the rain is on our side and clear on theirs,
> One must remain firm and absolutely not advance.

> Heaven weeps for the enemy as I deploy my troops.
> If there are no secret plots or other preparations,
> Keep the **cooks** <term>huotou (火頭); the military kitchen and logistics units</term> ready to protect the camp.

When the army sets out at night and sees the moon in the east, with clouds intersecting the moon: if the clouds appear to submerge the moon, it is auspicious to follow the direction of the clouds in battle. This is called the "Interaction of Clouds and Moon."

> Only then, upon the river, will your passage be successful and smooth.

If a rainbow drinks the water within a camp, it signifies bloodshed, desertion, and emptiness. The general will face calamity. Moving the camp will bring good fortune. If the camp is not moved, or if repairs and changes are not made, the outcome will be auspicious. <note>In ancient Chinese meteorology, rainbows were often seen as living creatures—celestial serpents or dragons—that descended to earth to drink. In a military context, this "drinking" was thought to exhaust the vitality of the location.</note>

### A Long Rainbow Drinking Water Inside the Camp

->The song says:<-

> When a long rainbow descends to drink the water within the camp,
> One sees bloodshed, disasters, and illnesses that never cease.
> Repair the camp and change its layout to avert the evil;
> Be cautious with fire and smoke to cleanse the place of blood.

If a rainbow drinks from a household’s property, its wells, or its ponds, that family will first experience "three ruins" <note>likely referring to the loss of wealth, status, and health</note>, but afterward will give birth to beautiful women and widows throughout nine generations of the clan.

### A Rainbow Drinking from a Household

->The song says:<-

> If it drinks the water of a household, it is an ill omen;
> At first comes misfortune and three ruins, but later things return to good.
> Beautiful women will surely be born, connecting the whole clan;
> Through nine generations, military protection and merit will shine brightly.

<column-break/>

When the army is marching and the wind blows so fiercely that trees are snapped and broken, blocking the road ahead: even if the wood is cleared, this is a sign of a prepared ambush. One must investigate this thoroughly.

### Ambushing Troops and Trees Broken by Wind

->The song says:<-

> Trees snapped in the front mean the enemy ahead is strong;
> If they block our rear, the rear of the army will suffer disaster.
> If this happens, advancing the front of the army will not be easy,
> Or the rear may be harmed, making a retreat difficult to withstand.

While the army is on the move, if a rainbow blocks the road ahead, one must immediately strike gongs and blow horns to perform a ritual of aversion <term>rang (禳); a ritual or sacrifice intended to ward off an impending evil or natural disaster</term>. Wait until the rainbow has dissipated before setting out again; this will ensure lasting good fortune.

### A Rainbow Blocking the Road

->The song says:<-

> A long rainbow cuts horizontally across the army’s path;
> Sound the gongs and blow the horns, and let the army halt.
> Wait until the rainbow has scattered before the troops march;
> Then, whether going North, South, East, or West, you may proceed as you wish.

If the army sees a long rainbow drinking water in front of them, it is ominous for the men and horses at the spot where the water is being drunk. One should halt and camp three to seven *li* <note>a Chinese mile, roughly 500 meters</note> away. When advancing again, take a different route to cross the water away from where the rainbow drank; thus, the calamity will be dissolved and the outcome will be auspicious.

### A Rainbow Drinking Water in Front of the Army

## If the army travels for ten days and it remains overcast without rain or sunlight, this indicates that the officers and soldiers will be uneasy. It also warns of the sign of ambushes and secret plots along the road. ->The song says:<-

> For ten days the sky is overcast, yet there is no rain at all;
> The soldiers and officers will face disaster, and their grain will rot on the path.
> If those of the "Gong" surname and the yellow banners lead the way,
> Only then can the soldiers find peace and the misfortune be dispelled. <note>original: 宮姓 "Gong surname." In ancient Chinese music and five-element theory, the "Gong" note corresponds to the Element of Earth and the color yellow, which were believed to provide stability against "overcast" or "water" related disasters.</note>

If the army encounters thick dust that covers people's clothes like spots of mud, this corresponds to a military disaster. It is advisable to halt and not advance; to engage in battle would be unlucky. If the dust clings to people like mud, the general should seek a resolution to the omen. ->The song says:<-

> The dark, thick dust is difficult to pierce through;
> If it clings to one's body, do not wait for luck to change.
> You will not be victorious in battle; it is better to seek a truce,
> Or else use secret stratagems to let information flow through.

While on the march or staying in camp, if you encounter "earth-hair," "stone-blood," or other strange colors, you should remain stationed. To go out and engage in battle will not be auspicious. <gloss>The sky rains earth and stones</gloss> <note>"Earth-hair" and "stone-blood" likely refer to unusual mold, moss, or mineral seepages that were interpreted as the earth "bleeding" or "growing hair," viewed as terrifying omens of nature out of balance.</note> ->The song says:<-

> When the heavens rain strange things, it is always an ill omen;
> The soldiers worry about disaster, and the general fears calamity.

<column-break/>

### If the army sees sickness on the march, choose another day; if you stay, you should prepare for battle; if you go out, you will perish.

If within the camp at night, star-like lights are seen upon the tips of weapons, but they disappear when brought before a lamp, this is the "Venus Defeat Star." It signifies winning first but losing later, and the general will face danger. To remedy this, take the weapon tip that showed the light and bury it in a direction that is auspicious for the current year. <note>Venus (Taibai) was the planet associated with war, metal, and execution. Its "light" clinging to weapons was seen as a parasitic energy that would exhaust the army's luck.</note> ->The song says:<-

> Within the army, the weapon tips shine like stars at night;
> Yet when brought before a lamp, they are no longer bright.
> This surely signifies victory first and then a certain defeat;
> Cut off the omen by burying the tip in an auspicious direction.

If blood is suddenly seen upon the tips of blades or swords in the army, it is a sign of defeat and death. Order all units to sharpen and organize their equipment immediately for great good fortune. ->The song says:<-

> When blood stains the blades, the soldiers find no advantage;
> Weakness, death, and disaster for the general bring seven taboos.
> Sharpen your equipment to suppress the evil;
> Furthermore, commencing maintenance work is the key secret.

If a lookout banner falls, it is a sign of worry that the battle line will suffer a setback. The direction in which the fallen banner's tip points is the source of the calamity; one must firmly fortify the city.

If [the signs] appear in other directions, hold your position firmly. Upon encountering a battle formation, do not engage.
When the mind is confused, one should use a bow to shoot two arrows. Such harm means that *Lingguang* <note>original: 凌光. Likely referring to a specific astral deity or the "Divine Light" associated with the Southern quadrant in Daoist military divination.</note> and others are not favorable for battle.
->The song says:<-

> The water boils and the river turns over; the people's minds are in chaos.
> The King's commands cannot pass through; it is difficult to govern.
> If you see this, you must order the arrows to be shot;
> The <term>Ritual Master</term> <note>original: 法師 "Fashi." A specialist in esoteric rituals and exorcisms within the army.</note> will naturally obtain the means to dispel the disaster.

If the well water within the military camp boils, worry that a conspiracy or thieves will arise from the exact East. Take one green stone weighing ten catties <note>A "catty" or *jin* is a traditional unit of weight, roughly 600 grams.</note>, smoke it with wine, and after it has boiled several times, throw it into the well to perform a <term>rite of exorcism</term> <note>original: 禳 "Rang." A ritual intended to avert or suppress an evil omen.</note>. ->The song says:<-

> If the well water boils over, there is a hidden evil;
> Smoke a green stone with wine and throw it into the boiling water.
> Perform the exorcism quickly according to the law to avoid disaster;
> Free yourself from the worry of internal and external treachery.

If the well inside the camp suddenly dries up, the morale will turn weak; fear that sudden troops will arrive and you will not win the battle. Bury five catties of raw iron inside the well. ->The song says:<-

> When the well water in the camp dries up;
> One must fear meeting treachery and losing one's power.

<column-break/>

If the <term>Great Banner</term> <note>original: 纛 "Dao." The primary ceremonial standard or "commander's flag" of the army, often carrying deep symbolic and spiritual weight.</note> should fall, the camp should cut it, take it, and bury it under the road at the camp gate. Trample over it as you pass, and the calamity will surely be removed. ->The song says:<-

> When the flag falls to the ground, my power is strong; <note>The text suggests that by performing the ritual burial and trampling, the commander "overpowers" the bad omen, turning it into a source of strength.</note>
> But if it simply falls toward the camp, my army will perish.
> Bury the flag and spear at the camp and trample over them;
> The military commander encountering this should consider it well.

Whether the army is on the march or in the camp, regardless of the four seasons, if thunder sounds behind the army, the troops have received Heaven’s help and Divine protection. It is a sign of advancing to achieve success and great victory. If it sounds in front of the army, it is advisable to station on the left or right; do not occupy the forward position. ->The song says:<-

> Deploying the ranks will surely result in a remarkable victory;
> When thunder follows the army, it vibrates the Great Leader.
> If it is in front of the army, stop fighting the enemy;
> Or there will be pestilence, bloodshed, and death upon the road.

If thunder and lightning strike objects while the army is marching or in camp, and if the nature of the objects corresponds to the Great General's <term>Natal Land</term> <note>original: 本命土地. The astrological direction or element associated with the General's birth year.</note>, then it is a sign of divine help from the *Tianchong* <note>original: 天冲 "Celestial Clash." One of the Nine Stars in Qimen Dunjia divination, usually associated with thunder, speed, and aggressive action.</note> deity. If it occurs in another direction, it is not advisable to lead the army out for attack; wait one month for it to be auspicious. ->The song says:<-

> Divine thunder and lightning assist the army's majesty;
> The plans for the current year and the passing year can then be carried out.

# Rhapsody on Auspicious Signs and Strange Anomalies

<note>original: 祥異賦 (Xiángyì Fù). In traditional Chinese philosophy, "Auspicious Signs" (Xiáng) refer to lucky omens, while "Strange Anomalies" (Yì) refer to bizarre or disastrous occurrences. Together, they represent the "Mandate of Heaven" signaling its approval or disapproval of a ruler's conduct.</note>

<term>Rhapsody (Fu): A classical Chinese literary form that sits between poetry and prose. It is known for its elaborate descriptions and was often used at court to praise the emperor or offer subtle political critiques.</term>

<summary>This is the title page of a classical Chinese poetic work concerning the interpretation of omens and celestial portents. Such texts were vital for understanding how historical figures interpreted natural disasters and lucky events as divine political feedback.</summary>

<keywords>Rhapsody, Fu, Omens, Anomalies, Mandate of Heaven, Chinese Poetry, Political Philosophy</keywords>
